concepts.name: Will · Skill · Opportunity
concepts.line: Every action needs at least two of three: wanting it, being able, and an open door.

concepts.name: The 2/3 Rule
concepts.line: Find the one missing pillar and push there — not everywhere.

concepts.name: The Capable Bystander
concepts.line: Skill and access without fire: no productivity hack fixes a missing why.

concepts.name: The Dreaming Sprinter
concepts.line: Desire plus an open door is the best place to learn anything.

concepts.name: The Competent Prisoner
concepts.line: When will and skill are full, the fight is structural, not personal.

concepts.name: Self-Efficacy
concepts.line: Believed skill, not actual skill, decides whether you even try.

concepts.name: The Map Is Not the Territory
concepts.line: Everything you know is a simplified map. Useful, never complete.

concepts.name: You See What You Aim At
concepts.line: Your goals decide what your eyes even notice.

concepts.name: Reframing
concepts.line: Same event, different frame, different body, different action.

concepts.name: Stress Mindset
concepts.line: Believing stress can fuel you changes what it does to you.

concepts.name: Pragmatic Truth
concepts.line: Judge an idea by what happens when you live by it.

concepts.name: Perceive → Appraise → Recalibrate
concepts.line: Run your mind like a good controller: predict, compare, adjust, repeat.

concepts.name: Fast & Slow Thinking
concepts.line: A quick hare and a careful owl share your skull. Know who's driving.

concepts.name: Anchoring
concepts.line: The first number you hear quietly drags every estimate after it.

concepts.name: Availability Bias
concepts.line: What's easy to remember feels more likely than it is.

concepts.name: Confirmation Bias
concepts.line: You hunt for evidence you're right. Try hunting for the opposite.

concepts.name: Loss Aversion
concepts.line: Losing $50 hurts about twice as much as winning $50 feels good.

concepts.name: Inversion
concepts.line: To get what you want, first list how to guarantee failure — then avoid it.

concepts.name: Second-Order Thinking
concepts.line: Ask 'and then what?' — twice.

concepts.name: Base Rates
concepts.line: Before the vivid story, ask: how often does this happen in general?

concepts.name: Feedback Loops
concepts.line: Reinforcing loops snowball; balancing loops hold steady. Spot which one you're in.

concepts.name: Delays
concepts.line: When results lag actions, people overcorrect. Patience is a systems skill.

concepts.name: Leverage Points
concepts.line: Small push, right place, big change. Usually the goal or the rules — not the numbers.

concepts.name: Fixes That Fail
concepts.line: The quick fix that relieves today often feeds tomorrow's problem.

concepts.name: Shifting the Burden
concepts.line: Relying on a crutch weakens the muscle that would have solved it.

concepts.name: The Habit Loop
concepts.line: Cue → craving → response → reward. Change any link, change the habit.

concepts.name: Identity-Based Habits
concepts.line: Every action is a vote for the person you're becoming.

concepts.name: 1% Compounding
concepts.line: 1% better daily is ~37× in a year. 1% worse is near zero.

concepts.name: The Two-Minute Rule
concepts.line: Make the start so small you can't say no.

concepts.name: Environment Design
concepts.line: Willpower is a weak lever. Rearrange the room instead.

concepts.name: Never Miss Twice
concepts.line: Missing once is an accident. Missing twice is the start of a new habit.

concepts.name: Name It to Tame It
concepts.line: 'Bad' is vague. 'Embarrassed and tired' is workable.

concepts.name: The Pause
concepts.line: Between trigger and reaction there's a gap. Widen it by three breaths.

concepts.name: Self-Compassion
concepts.line: Talk to yourself like you'd talk to a friend who's struggling.

concepts.name: Procrastination Is a Feeling Problem
concepts.line: We don't avoid tasks. We avoid the feeling the task gives us.

concepts.name: Emotional Contagion
concepts.line: Moods spread like weather fronts through rooms and group chats.

concepts.name: Start With Why
concepts.line: People commit to why you do it before what you do.

concepts.name: Meaning Through Responsibility
concepts.line: Pick up the heaviest load you can carry. Meaning is in the carrying.

concepts.name: Order & Chaos
concepts.line: Too much order is a cage; too much chaos is a flood. Live on the border.

concepts.name: Aim at Something
concepts.line: A worthy aim reorganizes what you see, do and endure.

concepts.name: Flow
concepts.line: Challenge slightly above skill + clear goals = time disappears.

concepts.name: Growth Mindset
concepts.line: Treating ability as trainable changes how you handle hard things.

concepts.name: The Power of 'Yet'
concepts.line: 'I can't do this' → 'I can't do this yet.' One word, new door.

concepts.name: Grit
concepts.line: Passion plus perseverance for long-term goals predicts more than talent alone.

concepts.name: Deliberate Practice
concepts.line: Practice at the edge of your ability, with feedback, on one weakness.

concepts.name: Mistakes as Data
concepts.line: A mistake is the most precise feedback you'll get today.

concepts.name: The Cookie Jar of Wins
concepts.line: Keep proof of what you've survived. Reach in when it gets hard.

concepts.name: Quitting Wisely
concepts.line: Grit isn't never quitting. It's quitting the right things on purpose.

concepts.name: Three Kinds of Conversation
concepts.line: Every talk is practical, emotional or social. Match the kind, or miss each other.

concepts.name: Looping for Understanding
concepts.line: Repeat back what you heard, ask if you got it right. People soften when proven heard.

concepts.name: Introvert / Extrovert Energy
concepts.line: It's not shy vs. loud — it's where you recharge.

concepts.name: Shared Stories
concepts.line: Money, nations, rules: humans cooperate at scale by believing the same stories.

concepts.name: Steelmanning
concepts.line: State the other side so well they'd say 'yes, exactly' — then disagree.

concepts.name: Asking for Help Is Brave
concepts.line: The bravest thing you can say is often 'help'.

concepts.name: Deep Work
concepts.line: Undistracted focus on hard things is rare — and therefore valuable.

concepts.name: Attention Residue
concepts.line: Each switch leaves part of your mind behind on the last task.

concepts.name: Sleep Saves Your Learning
concepts.line: Sleep is when the brain files today's learning. Skip it, lose it.

concepts.name: The Scroll Loop
concepts.line: Variable rewards keep thumbs moving long after joy has left.

concepts.name: Boredom Is a Signal
concepts.line: Boredom isn't empty — it's your mind asking for a better goal.

concepts.name: One-Way vs Two-Way Doors
concepts.line: Most decisions are reversible. Decide those fast; slow down only for the one-way doors.

concepts.name: Regret Minimization
concepts.line: Picture yourself at 80. Which choice would you regret not making?

concepts.name: The Pre-Mortem
concepts.line: Imagine it failed. Now explain why — before it happens.

concepts.name: Expected Value
concepts.line: Odds × payoff. Good decisions can have bad outcomes — judge the decision.

concepts.name: Opportunity Cost
concepts.line: The real price of a yes is the best thing you said no to.

concepts.name: Circle of Competence
concepts.line: Know the edge of what you know — that's where mistakes live.

concepts.name: Dichotomy of Control
concepts.line: Some things are up to you, some aren't. Spend energy only on the first.

concepts.name: Circle of Influence
concepts.line: Proactive people work inside what they can influence; it grows.

concepts.name: The Golden Mean
concepts.line: Courage sits between cowardice and recklessness. Virtue is calibrated.

concepts.name: Knowing You Don't Know
concepts.line: The wisest person in Athens was the one who knew what he didn't know.

concepts.name: Amor Fati
concepts.line: Don't just accept what happened. Use it as fuel.

concepts.name: This Too Shall Pass
concepts.line: Feelings and fortunes are weather, not climate.

concepts.name: Begin With the End in Mind
concepts.line: Write your own eulogy, then live backwards from it.

cards.hook: Think of one goal you keep not doing. Which part is missing?
cards.title: Will, Skill, Opportunity

questions.q: I genuinely want this, even when nobody is watching.
If it got hard or boring, I'd happily drop it.
I could do a rough first version of this today.
I'd need someone to show me where to even start.
I have the time, access and permission to begin.
Something outside me (money, rules, a gatekeeper) blocks the way.

W.name: The Dreamer
W.text: The fire is real, but there's no skill or door yet. Don't wait for both: pick the one that's cheaper to build first, usually a small skill.

S.name: The Idle Expert
S.text: You can do it, but you don't want it and nothing invites you in. Ask whether this goal is truly yours, or borrowed from someone else.

O.name: The Open Door
O.text: The way is open, but there's no want and no know-how yet. An open door is a gift; check if anything behind it sparks curiosity.

SW.name: The Competent Prisoner
SW.text: You want it and you can do it, but the door is locked. That's structural, not a flaw in you. Find another door, or build one with others.

OW.name: The Dreaming Sprinter
OW.text: Desire plus an open door: the best place to learn anything. Your job now is practice, in small, honest reps with feedback.

OS.name: The Capable Bystander
OS.text: Everything is in place except the fire. No productivity trick fixes a missing why. Find the reason that would make this matter to you.

OSW.name: Full Agency
OSW.text: All three pillars are lit. The only thing left is to start. Put the first 10 minutes on your calendar.

results.name: The Seed
results.text: Nothing is lit yet, and that's fine: every agent starts here. Pick the easiest pillar to grow this week. Two of three is enough to move.

cards.insight: Action needs a want, an ability and an open door. Most stuck goals are missing one, and pushing harder on the ones you have rarely helps. Naming the gap tells you where to aim.
cards.model: Stuck? Don't push everywhere. Find the missing pillar: Will, Skill or Opportunity.
cards.try_today: Write your goal at the top of a page, then one line each for W, S and O. Circle the weakest and take one step on it.

source.work: QUMNI WSO Framework; builds on Self-Determination Theory and self-efficacy research

cards.hook: A gifted kid grows up with no instruments. What happens to the gift?
cards.title: Talent needs a door

game.prompt: Picture a child with a gift for music and a hunger to play, born in a place with no instruments, no teachers and no time off work. Does her talent show up anyway?
choices: Yes, real talent always finds a way
Probably not, or only in pieces
game.reveal: Usually it never shows, or only in pieces. Will and early skill are there, but the door is shut. Many gifted people never got to do their work because they lacked access, time or permission. Gifts are spread widely; open doors are not.

cards.insight: We love stories where grit beats everything, but they hide the many who had grit and no door. Seeing the missing pillar is kinder and more accurate than blaming people for not trying.
cards.model: Talent and drive are necessary, not sufficient. Someone has to open, or build, the door.
cards.try_today: Think of one person whose skill you admire but who lacks a door. Send them one lead, intro or resource today.

source.work: QUMNI WSO Framework; Giddens, The Constitution of Society (1984)

cards.hook: You have one hour to help a stuck friend. Where do you spend it?
cards.title: Push the missing pillar

steps.scenario: Ana loves cooking and is great at it. She wants to start a supper club but has no space to host it. You help by…

options.text: Sending her a cooking masterclass
options.feedback: Kind, but her skill is already strong. More of what she has won't unlock the door.

options.text: Giving her a pep talk about following her dream
options.feedback: Her will is already on fire. Encouragement is nice but it isn't the bottleneck.

options.text: Asking a café owner you know if she can use their space on Mondays
options.feedback: Yes. Will and Skill are lit; Opportunity is missing. One door does more than ten pep talks.

steps.scenario: Leo has free time, a laptop and a coding course already paid for. He keeps saying he 'should' learn to code but never opens it. You…

options.text: Ask what he'd actually build if he could code, and why it matters to him
options.feedback: Yes. Skill can be learned and the door is open; the gap is Will. A real reason does more than a schedule.

options.text: Make him a strict study timetable
options.feedback: Structure helps once he wants it. Right now it would be a plan for something he doesn't care about yet.

options.text: Buy him a second, better course
options.feedback: He already has the door. A bigger door won't make him walk through it.

cards.insight: Two pillars out of three is usually enough to move; the third is where your effort pays off most. People often push the pillar they already have because it feels comfortable.
cards.model: Push the one weak pillar, not all three. Small help in the right spot beats big help elsewhere.
cards.try_today: Ask someone stuck: 'Is it wanting, knowing how, or access?' Then offer help only on the answer they give.

source.work: QUMNI WSO Framework: Will, Skill, Opportunity

cards.hook: Two of three is enough to move. Can you spot who's about to?
cards.title: Spot the 2 out of 3

game.prompt: Does this person have at least two pillars lit?

items.text: Mia wants to run a 5K, has never run, and there's a park next door.
items.why: Will + Opportunity. Skill can be built on the way: start with walk-run intervals.

items.text: Sam is a trained nurse, burned out, with job offers he doesn't want.
items.why: Skill + Opportunity. Burnout is real: rest and a renewed why come before more offers.

items.text: Jo dreams of acting, has never tried, and no theatre is nearby.
items.why: Only Will. Build one more pillar first, like an online class or a local reading group.

items.text: Raj can fix bikes, loves it, and a neighbour just asked for help.
items.why: All three. Full agency: he only needs to say yes.

items.text: Lee has a free gym pass but no interest and no idea how to train.
items.why: Only Opportunity. An open door alone doesn't move anyone.

cards.insight: When two pillars are lit, action becomes possible and the third can often be grown on the way. When only one is lit, it usually helps more to add a second pillar than to push harder on the one you have.
cards.model: Two pillars make motion possible. One pillar alone usually stalls.
cards.try_today: List three goals. Count the lit pillars for each. Start the one with the most lit today.

source.work: QUMNI WSO Framework: Will, Skill, Opportunity

cards.hook: Is it really laziness, or do you just not care about this goal?
cards.title: The Capable Bystander

questions.q: When I picture finishing this goal, I feel…
If nobody would ever know I quit, I would…
The reason for this goal mostly came from…
When I describe it to a friend, I say…

zones.label: Borrowed goal
zones.text: This goal may belong to someone else. That isn't a character flaw. Either find your own reason inside it, or consider letting it go.

zones.label: Flickering fire
zones.text: Some want, some 'should'. Connect the goal to one person or value you truly care about and see if it grows.

zones.label: Real fire
zones.text: Your will is real. If you're still stuck, look at Skill or Opportunity instead of blaming motivation.

cards.insight: When skill and access are there but nothing happens, the missing piece is usually a reason that is truly yours. Goals driven by your own values tend to last longer than goals driven by pressure. If nothing has felt worth wanting for weeks, talk to someone you trust.
cards.model: No productivity hack fixes a missing why. Find your reason, or free yourself from the goal.
cards.try_today: Finish this sentence in writing: 'This matters to me because…' If you can't, cross the goal off or hand it back.

source.work: Deci & Ryan, Self-Determination Theory (1985); Ryan & Deci, American Psychologist (2000)

cards.hook: You want it and the door is open. So why aren't you better yet?
cards.title: The Dreaming Sprinter

game.prompt: Put a good practice session in order
items: Pick one small sub-skill
Practice just beyond your comfort zone
Get fast, honest feedback
Adjust and try again
game.explain: This is the core loop of deliberate practice: narrow focus, a stretch, feedback, then correction. Repeating what you can already do feels good but teaches little.

cards.insight: Desire plus an open door is a great place to learn, but hours alone don't build skill; focused practice with feedback helps more. The '10,000-hour rule' is a myth Ericsson himself rejected, and practice explains only part of skill differences.
cards.model: Skill grows at the edge: one sub-skill, a stretch, feedback, adjust, repeat.
cards.try_today: Choose one tiny part of a skill you want. Do 5 focused minutes on only that, then ask someone for one piece of feedback.

source.work: Ericsson & Pool, Peak (2016); Macnamara et al., Psychological Science (2014)

cards.hook: You're trying harder and harder. What if the wall isn't you?
cards.title: The Competent Prisoner

game.prompt: Where's the blocker?

items.text: The job you want requires a licence your country won't recognise.
items.why: A rule, not a flaw. Look for bridging programmes or roles that don't need the licence.

items.text: You keep phoning it in on a project you no longer care about.
items.why: That's Will. Reconnect with a reason or renegotiate the project.

items.text: You can only study after 11pm because of two shifts.
items.why: Time is Opportunity. Shrink the task or trade for a better slot, not more willpower.

items.text: You don't know how to write a cover letter yet.
items.why: That's Skill, and it's learnable fast with templates and feedback.

items.text: Nobody in your field hires people without a referral.
items.why: A gate. Build doors: meet people, join communities, ask for intros.

cards.insight: When will and skill are full, more effort on yourself can backfire into self-blame. Some walls are rules, money, time or gatekeepers. Seeing that is not an excuse; it tells you to change the setup or find another door.
cards.model: If you want it and can do it but still can't, the fight is structural. Change the setup, not yourself.
cards.try_today: Name one outside blocker on a goal. Write two other doors around it: another route, person, or place.

source.work: Giddens, The Constitution of Society (1984); Bourdieu, The Forms of Capital (1986)

cards.hook: A friend says 'I'm just not a speaker.' What actually helps?
cards.title: Belief built by doing

steps.scenario: Your friend dreads speaking up in meetings and says 'I'm just not that kind of person.' You…

options.text: Tell them they're amazing and will be fine
options.feedback: Warm, and encouragement does help a bit. But words fade fast when the moment comes.

options.text: Suggest they share one prepared sentence in the next meeting
options.feedback: Yes. A small success they create themselves is the strongest source of 'I can'. Then make the next step a bit bigger.

options.text: Send them a video of a famous speaker
options.feedback: Watching others helps most when the model is similar to them. A star can feel out of reach.

options.text: Say some people just aren't speakers
options.feedback: Meant kindly, but it locks the belief in place. Belief in what you can do changes with experience.

cards.insight: Bandura found that whether you even try depends on believing you can, not only on your real skill. The strongest builder of that belief is a small success of your own. Encouragement, role models and a calm body help too.
cards.model: Believed skill decides if you try. Build belief with small wins you earn, not with pep talks alone.
cards.try_today: Pick something you think you're 'bad at'. Do the smallest possible version of it once today and notice that you did it.

source.work: Self-efficacy: Toward a unifying theory of behavioral change (1977)

cards.hook: Where does your 'I can do this' actually come from?
cards.title: Your four sources of belief

questions.q: I can remember recent times I did something hard and it worked.
I often finish small things I start.
I know someone like me who has done what I want to do.
People I trust tell me they think I can do it.
When I'm nervous, I read it as my body getting ready, not as a sign I'll fail.

advice.0: Lowest on own wins? Set a goal so small you can't fail, finish it, and write it down. Stack a few this week.
advice.1: Lowest on role models? Find one person a step or two ahead of you, not a superstar, and learn how they started.
advice.2: Lowest on encouragement? Tell one supportive person your goal and ask them to check in with you in a week.
advice.3: Lowest on calm body? Before a hard task, take three slow breaths and say 'my body is getting ready.'

cards.insight: Bandura described four sources of self-efficacy: your own successes, seeing similar people succeed, encouragement, and how you read your body's signals. Your own wins usually count most, but the others can fill a gap.
cards.model: Belief in yourself is built from four sources. Find your weakest and feed it.
cards.try_today: Write down three things you did well in the past month. Read the list right before your next hard task.

source.work: Bandura, Self-Efficacy: The Exercise of Control (1997); Jamieson et al., arousal reappraisal studies (2010)

cards.hook: When did you last think about one hard thing for 60 minutes straight?
cards.title: Deep Work

questions.q: When a hard task gets uncomfortable, I usually…

options.label: Stay with it until it gives a little

questions.q: My notifications while I work are…

options.label: All on, I like being reachable
Off until I choose to look

questions.q: My most important work happens…

options.label: In the gaps between other things
Whenever I find a quiet moment
In a block I protect on purpose

questions.q: At the end of a busy day I often feel…

options.label: Exhausted, but unsure what I made
Tired, and I can point to progress

zones.label: Mostly shallow
zones.text: Your days are full of reacting. That's normal in a ping-everywhere world, not a flaw. One protected block a day would change your output more than any app.

zones.label: Mixed
zones.text: You go deep sometimes, but it's luck more than design. Pick the time, the place and the one task in advance and it gets far more reliable.

zones.label: Deep-leaning
zones.text: You already guard your focus. Next level: make the block longer by 10 minutes, or tackle a harder problem inside it.

cards.insight: Newport argues that focus on hard things without distraction is getting rarer, so it's getting more valuable. It's a skill, not a personality type. You train it by scheduling it and by sitting through the first few uncomfortable minutes.
cards.model: Busy is not the same as productive. Protect one block for the work that actually moves things.
cards.try_today: Pick one task, set a 25-minute timer, put your phone in another room, and work until it rings.

source.work: Deep Work (2016)

cards.hook: Half your to-do list could be done half-asleep. Which half?
cards.title: Deep vs. Shallow Tasks

game.prompt: Does this need your full brain?

items.text: Replying 'sounds good!' to an email
items.why: Easy to do while distracted, and easy for anyone to do.

items.text: Writing the first draft of a tough essay
items.why: Needs you to hold many ideas at once. Interruptions wreck it.

items.text: Learning a new chord on the guitar
items.why: New skills need focused attention on the exact part you get wrong.

items.text: Booking a dentist appointment
items.why: Necessary, but low-thought. Batch it with other small chores.

items.text: Planning how to fix a money problem
items.why: Hard trade-offs need quiet thinking, not 30-second bursts.

items.text: Tidying your desktop files
items.why: Feels productive, uses little brain. A classic stand-in for hard work.

cards.insight: Shallow tasks are real and need doing, but they are easy to copy and easy to do tired. Deep tasks create new value and need your fresh hours. Most people spend their best energy on the shallow pile first.
cards.model: Give your freshest hour to the deep pile. Batch the shallow pile for when you're tired.
cards.try_today: Write tomorrow's list in two columns, deep and shallow, and schedule one deep item before you open email.

source.work: Deep Work (2016)

cards.hook: How long do you stay on one screen before switching? Guess.
cards.title: Attention Residue

game.question: In Gloria Mark's recent workplace studies, how many seconds did people stay on one screen, on average, before switching?
game.explain: About 47 seconds on average in her studies from 2016 onward, down from about 2.5 minutes in 2004 (Mark, Attention Span, 2023). Sophie Leroy separately found that after a switch, part of your mind stays stuck on the task you just left.

cards.insight: Leroy called it attention residue: after a switch, part of your mind is still on the last task, so you think less sharply on the new one. Quick 'just checking' glances look free, but they leave a trail. Finishing, or writing a note on where you stopped, helps you let go.
cards.model: Every switch leaves a bit of you behind. Fewer switches means more of you shows up.
cards.try_today: Before you switch tasks, write one line: where you stopped and the next step. Then switch.

source.work: Leroy, Why is it so hard to do my work? (2009); Mark, Attention Span (2023)

cards.hook: It's 1 a.m. before a big exam. Do you cram or close the book?
cards.title: Sleep Saves Your Learning

steps.scenario: Exam at 9 a.m. You've studied all evening. It's 1 a.m. and you feel you've only half got it. You…

options.text: Do one quick review of the key points, then sleep
options.feedback: Smart. A short review before sleep, then real sleep, gives your brain both the material and the time to store it.

options.text: Pull an all-nighter to cover everything
options.feedback: Understandable panic. But without sleep, recall and focus usually drop, so extra hours can cost more than they add.

options.text: Sleep, then cram at 6 a.m.
options.feedback: Better than no sleep. But cutting the last hours of the night trims REM-rich sleep, which research links to memory too.

steps.scenario: You're learning a new skill this month: a language, a sport, an instrument. The best plan is…

options.text: Practice once a week for three hours
options.feedback: Better than nothing, but one long session gets only one night of sleep to lock it in.

options.text: Practice 20 minutes most days, sleeping well between
options.feedback: Yes. Spaced practice plus nights of sleep lets the brain replay and file what you learned.

options.text: Practice late at night to save time
options.feedback: Fine sometimes, but if it eats into sleep, you may lose the gains you just made.

cards.insight: Lots of research shows sleep helps the brain strengthen and file what you learned that day. Learning is the study plus the nights after. Walker's book made this famous, though critics say some of its wider claims go beyond the evidence.
cards.model: Learning = practice + sleep. Cutting sleep to study more often means remembering less.
cards.try_today: Set an alarm 30 minutes before your bedtime tonight that means: screens down, lights low.

source.work: Stickgold, Sleep-dependent memory consolidation, Nature (2005); Walker, Why We Sleep (2017)

cards.hook: You opened the app for 'one second.' Can you trace what happened?
cards.title: The Scroll Loop

game.prompt: Put the scroll loop in order
items: A small itch: boredom, worry, an awkward pause
Thumb reaches for the phone, almost on its own
Unpredictable feed: dull, dull, then something great
A short hit of relief or novelty
The itch is still there, so you keep going
game.explain: The feed works like a slot machine: you never know when the next good post comes, so you keep pulling. The relief is real but brief, and it doesn't fix the itch that started it.

cards.insight: Scrolling is a habit loop driven by unpredictable rewards, which are the hardest kind to stop chasing. You're not weak; the design is strong. Haidt argues heavy phone use harms young people, but researchers still debate how big that effect is.
cards.model: If the reward is random, the habit is sticky. Break the loop at the itch, not the thumb.
cards.try_today: Next time you reach for your phone, pause and name the itch in one word (bored, tense, lonely). Then decide.

source.work: Ferster & Skinner, Schedules of Reinforcement (1957); Haidt, The Anxious Generation (2024)

cards.hook: Two pigeons. One gets food every peck, one at random. Who quits last?
cards.title: Why Random Rewards Hook Us

game.prompt: Two pigeons learn to peck a button for food. Pigeon A gets food every single peck. Pigeon B gets food at random, unpredictable pecks. Then the food stops completely. Which pigeon keeps pecking longer?
game.reveal: Pigeon B, by a lot. Behaviour rewarded on an unpredictable schedule is much harder to extinguish (Ferster & Skinner). Feeds, inboxes and slot machines all pay out unpredictably.

cards.insight: When rewards are predictable, you notice fast when they stop. When they're random, every empty pull feels like 'maybe next time.' That's why apps with refresh-for-something-new are so hard to put down.
cards.model: Random rewards build the stickiest habits. Make the good stuff predictable and the feed boring.
cards.try_today: Turn off notifications for one app that pings you at random, and check it at two set times instead.

source.work: Schedules of Reinforcement (1957)

cards.hook: Alone with your thoughts for 15 minutes, or a mild shock? Guess.
cards.title: Boredom Is a Signal

game.question: In a 2014 study, people sat alone with nothing to do for 15 minutes, with a button that gave a mild electric shock. What % of men shocked themselves at least once?
game.explain: 12 of 18 men (67%) and 6 of 24 women (25%) pressed it at least once, and all of them had earlier said they'd pay money to avoid that shock (Wilson et al., Science, 2014). Small samples, so treat the exact numbers loosely.

cards.insight: Many of us would rather feel something unpleasant than feel nothing. Researchers like Danckert and Eastwood describe boredom as a signal that what you're doing doesn't engage you. Listened to, it can point you toward a better goal instead of a quick escape.
cards.model: Boredom is a question, not a void: 'What would actually be worth my attention right now?'
cards.try_today: Next time you feel bored, wait two minutes before grabbing your phone and ask: what would I like to be doing?

source.work: Out of My Skull (2020); Wilson et al., Science (2014)

cards.hook: Your advice was good. So why did they get more upset?
cards.title: Three Kinds of Conversation

steps.scenario: Your friend says: 'My boss rewrote my whole report in front of everyone.' You reply…

options.text: Next time, send him a draft a day early.
options.feedback: Solid advice — for a practical talk. But this one sounds like it's about feelings first. Solutions land better after they feel heard.

options.text: In front of everyone? That sounds humiliating.
options.feedback: Yes. This is an emotional conversation. Naming the feeling tells them you're on the same channel.

options.text: My boss does that too, it's so annoying.
options.feedback: Friendly instinct, but it moves the spotlight to you. Stay on their story a bit longer.

steps.scenario: Later they say: 'OK, I'm calmer. What should I actually do on Monday?' Now you…

options.text: Keep validating: 'That must have felt awful.'
options.feedback: Kind, but they just switched channels. They're asking for a plan now.

options.text: Offer two concrete options and ask which fits.
options.feedback: Right. The talk turned practical, so you turned with it. Matching is a moving target.

options.text: Ask what this says about who they are at work.
options.feedback: That's a social/identity question. Could matter later — but they asked for a next step.

cards.insight: Most talks are one of three kinds: practical (what should we do?), emotional (how do we feel?), or social (who are we?). Advice given in an emotional talk often misses. Notice which kind you're in — and when it switches.
cards.model: Ask: is this about solving, feeling, or identity? Then answer in that same channel.
cards.try_today: In your next real conversation, silently label it practical, emotional, or social before you reply.

source.work: Supercommunicators (2024)

cards.hook: Want someone to calm down? Stop trying to convince them.
cards.title: Looping for Understanding

steps.scenario: Your partner snaps: 'You never help with the dishes!' You actually did them twice this week. You say…

options.text: That's not true, I did them Tuesday and Thursday.
options.feedback: Accurate — and it will probably start a fact fight. They don't feel heard yet, so facts sound like defense.

options.text: It sounds like you feel you're carrying most of the housework. Is that right?
options.feedback: That's a loop: repeat the heart of it, then check. You can share your facts after they say 'yes, exactly.'

options.text: Let's not do this right now.
options.feedback: Taking a break can be wise. But without a loop first, it can feel like a door closing.

steps.scenario: They answer: 'Not exactly — it's that I always have to ask.' You…

options.text: Ah, so it's less the dishes and more having to be the one who notices. Right?
options.feedback: Perfect. A loop that gets corrected isn't a failure — it's the loop working. Now you know the real issue.

options.text: Well, you could just ask nicely.
options.feedback: Understandable reflex, but it skips past what they just told you. Loop once more.

cards.insight: Looping means: ask, repeat back what you heard in your own words, then check if you got it right. People soften when they're proven heard — not just told 'I hear you.' Getting corrected is part of the method.
cards.model: Ask → say it back in your words → 'Did I get that right?' → repeat until they say yes.
cards.try_today: In one conversation today, say back what you heard and ask 'Did I get that right?' before giving your view.

source.work: Supercommunicators (2024); Rogers & Farson, Active Listening (1957)

cards.hook: 'I hear you' is not proof. Can you build the real thing?
cards.title: The Loop, Step by Step

game.prompt: Put the steps of looping for understanding in order
items: Ask a real question
Listen without planning your reply
Say back the core of it in your own words
Ask: 'Did I get that right?'
Adjust if they correct you
game.explain: The key is the check at the end. Summarizing without asking is still a guess. Asking turns your guess into shared understanding.

cards.insight: Listening is invisible; looping makes it visible. The person hears their idea in your words and gets a chance to fix it. That moment of 'yes, that's it' is often when tension drops.
cards.model: Understanding isn't what you feel — it's what the other person confirms.
cards.try_today: Pick one person today and do one full loop, ending with 'Did I get that right?'

source.work: Supercommunicators (2024); Rogers & Farson, Active Listening (1957)

cards.hook: After a great party, do you feel charged up or drained?
cards.title: Where You Recharge

questions.q: After a long day of meetings, I want…

options.label: A quiet room and no talking

questions.q: When I have a hard problem, I…

options.label: Talk it out to figure it out

questions.q: A free Saturday with no plans feels…
In a loud, busy room I…

zones.label: Introvert-leaning
zones.text: You probably recharge best in quiet. That's not shyness — you can be warm and bold and still need solitude to refuel.

zones.label: Ambivert zone
zones.text: Like many people, you sit near the middle. Your need for people vs. quiet may shift with sleep, stress, and who's around.

zones.label: Extrovert-leaning
zones.text: You likely get energy from people and stimulation. Quiet focus may need a bit more structure for you to enjoy.

cards.insight: Introversion isn't shyness; it's mostly about how much stimulation feels good. Most people land near the middle, not at the poles. 'Recharge' is a handy lens, but researchers still debate what extraversion really measures.
cards.model: Not shy vs. loud — notice what drains you and what refuels you, then plan around it.
cards.try_today: Look at tomorrow's schedule and add one 10-minute recharge block that fits your end of the spectrum.

source.work: Quiet (2012); Psychological Types (1921)

cards.hook: If every human vanished tonight, would your cash be worth a cent?
cards.title: Shared Stories

game.prompt: Would it still exist if no human believed in it?

items.text: The value of a 100-dollar bill
items.why: The paper stays. Its value lives in what millions of people agree to accept.

items.text: A mountain
items.why: Rock doesn't need anyone's belief. The name 'Everest' does, though.

items.text: A country's border
items.why: Rivers are real; the line on the map is an agreement people keep.

items.text: A company like Google
items.why: Harari's example: a company exists in law and shared belief, not in its buildings.

items.text: Gravity
items.why: It pulls whether anyone believes or not.

items.text: Your birthday being 'your day'
items.why: The Earth's orbit is real; the meaning of the date is a story we share.

cards.insight: Harari argues humans cooperate in huge numbers because we believe the same stories — money, laws, nations. 'Fiction' doesn't mean fake or bad: these stories are tools. The trick is remembering they can be rewritten.
cards.model: Some things are rocks, some are agreements. Agreements can be questioned — and changed.
cards.try_today: Name one 'rule' you follow today and ask: is this a rock or an agreement? Who could change it?

source.work: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind (2011)

cards.hook: Can you argue the other side so well they'd thank you?
cards.title: Steelmanning

steps.scenario: Your friend thinks phones should be banned in schools. You disagree. Which reply is a steelman?

options.text: So you think teens are too dumb to handle a phone?
options.feedback: That's a strawman — a weaker version that's easy to knock down. They'd likely just get annoyed.

options.text: You're worried phones pull kids' attention away from learning and from each other, and a clear rule is easier than constant fights. Fair?
options.feedback: Steelman. It's their best version, in words they'd agree with. Now your disagreement will actually be heard.

options.text: Whatever, people said the same about TV.
options.feedback: Might be a real point later, but it skips their argument instead of meeting it.

steps.scenario: They say: 'Yes, exactly.' Now you…

options.text: Say where you agree, then share your concern about emergencies and teaching phone skills.
options.feedback: Great. Agreement first, then disagreement. This is close to Rapoport's rules as Dennett describes them.

options.text: Say 'Great, but you're wrong because…'
options.feedback: You earned the floor, so don't spend it on 'you're wrong.' Start with what you share.

cards.insight: A strawman attacks the weakest version of a view. A steelman restates the strongest one first. It makes you fairer, makes others listen, and sometimes shows you that you were the one missing something.
cards.model: Before you disagree, state their view so well they say 'yes, exactly.'
cards.try_today: Pick a view you disagree with and write its strongest case in 3 sentences — as if you believed it.

source.work: Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking (2013)

cards.hook: Fair criticism has 4 steps. Most of us jump straight to step 4.
cards.title: Rapoport's Rules

game.prompt: Order the steps for criticizing someone's view fairly
items: Restate their view so clearly they wish they'd said it that way
List the points where you agree
Mention anything you learned from them
Only then, offer your criticism
game.explain: Daniel Dennett popularized these as 'Rapoport's Rules,' crediting the game theorist Anatol Rapoport. By step 4, the other person is far more ready to listen.

cards.insight: Criticism lands better after the other person feels understood and respected. These rules slow you down just enough to check you're arguing with their real view — not one you invented.
cards.model: Restate → agree → learn → then critique. Earn the right to disagree.
cards.try_today: Next time you disagree in a chat or meeting, do steps 1 and 2 out loud before your point.

source.work: Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking (2013)

cards.hook: You think people will say no if you ask for help. Want the real odds?
cards.title: Asking for Help Is Brave

game.prompt: In a study, people had to ask strangers to fill out a short form. To get 5 yeses, how many did they guess they'd need to ask?
choices: About as many as it took
About twice as many as it took
game.reveal: They guessed about twice as many as it took. Strangers were far more willing to help than askers expected (Flynn & Lake, 2008); later studies by Vanessa Bohns found the same.

cards.insight: We tend to underestimate how often others will say yes — partly because we focus on the cost of helping, while they feel the awkwardness of saying no. Asking isn't weakness; it's often what lets connection start.
cards.model: Others say yes more than you predict. 'Help' is a short, brave word.
cards.try_today: Ask one person for a small, specific bit of help today — and notice how they actually respond.

source.work: Flynn & Lake, 'If You Need Help, Just Ask' (2008); The Boy, the Mole, the Fox and the Horse (2019)

cards.hook: You spent 40 minutes picking a lunch spot. Was that door locked?
cards.title: One-Way vs Two-Way Doors

game.prompt: If this goes wrong, can you walk back through the door?

items.text: Trying a new gym class this week
items.why: Hate it? Don't go next week. Cheap to undo, so decide fast.

items.text: Getting a face tattoo
items.why: Hard and painful to reverse. This one deserves slow thinking.

items.text: Picking a paint color for your room
items.why: Paint is cheap. A weekend fixes a bad call.

items.text: Quitting a stable job with no savings
items.why: Hard to walk back. Slow down, gather info, maybe build a buffer first.

items.text: Testing a new morning routine for a week
items.why: A one-week experiment is the definition of reversible.

items.text: Saying something cruel in an argument
items.why: Words can be forgiven, but rarely unsaid. Pause before this door.

cards.insight: Most choices are two-way doors: if they go wrong, you can step back. Treating them like life-or-death costs time and energy. Save your careful thinking for the few doors that lock behind you.
cards.model: Ask 'Can I undo this?' Reversible: decide fast and learn. Irreversible: slow down.
cards.try_today: Pick one choice you've been stalling on. If it's reversible, decide it in the next 5 minutes and treat it as a test.

source.work: Amazon shareholder letter (2015)

cards.hook: Do you treat a menu like a marriage? Let's see where you land.
cards.title: How You Weigh Small Choices

game.right: Fast on small, slow on big

questions.q: Choosing a show to watch tonight, I usually…

options.label: Scroll for 20+ minutes and feel unsure
Pick one in a couple of minutes; I can switch

questions.q: Before a big move (new city, new career), I…

options.label: Jump in on a gut feeling
Take time, talk to people who've done it

questions.q: When a small choice turns out wrong, I…
When buying something with free returns, I…

options.label: Buy the good-enough one and test it

zones.label: Over-deliberator
zones.text: You give small choices big-choice energy. That's tiring. Try deadlines for reversible decisions and save your care for the big ones.

zones.label: Mixed
zones.text: Sometimes you sort well, sometimes small things eat your time. The quick test 'Can I undo this?' will tip you the right way.

zones.label: Door-sorter
zones.text: You move fast where it's safe and slow where it matters. Keep checking that 'fast' never sneaks onto a one-way door.

cards.insight: Good deciders aren't always slow or fast. They match speed to stakes. Barry Schwartz's research found people who always hunt for the best option (maximizers) tend, on average, to feel less satisfied than 'good enough' pickers, though later studies show mixed results.
cards.model: Match your decision speed to how reversible the choice is, not how anxious it makes you.
cards.try_today: Set a 2-minute timer for your next small choice (food, show, outfit). When it rings, pick and don't look back.

source.work: Amazon shareholder letter (2015); The Paradox of Choice (2004)

cards.hook: You're 80, in a rocking chair. Which choice still stings?
cards.title: The 80-Year-Old Test

game.prompt: Look back from age 80. Which hurts more over the years: the risks you took that failed, or the chances you never took?
game.reveal: In the short run, people regret mistakes they made. Over a lifetime, the regrets that last are mostly about what they didn't do (Gilovich & Medvec, 1995). Daniel Pink's World Regret Survey found 'boldness regrets' among the most common.

cards.insight: Failed attempts hurt, then fade: you learn, you explain them, you move on. Untaken chances stay open in your mind as 'what if'. Jeff Bezos used this test in 1994 to leave a secure job and start Amazon. Of course, it's a lens, not a license for reckless bets.
cards.model: From age 80, inaction usually hurts longer than a failed try. Let that tip close calls toward action.
cards.try_today: Write down one thing you'd regret never trying. Then write the smallest first step you could take this week.

source.work: The experience of regret (Psychological Review, 1995); The Power of Regret (2022)

cards.hook: Your plan already failed. It's a year from now. Why did it?
cards.title: The Pre-Mortem

game.prompt: Put the pre-mortem steps in order.
items: Describe the plan in one sentence
Imagine it's a year later and it failed badly
Write every reason it failed, alone and fast
Share the reasons and spot the biggest risks
Change the plan to block the top risks
game.explain: Assuming failure has already happened frees you to name problems you'd normally avoid saying out loud. Writing alone first stops the loudest voice from setting the list.

cards.insight: A post-mortem explains a failure after it's too late. A pre-mortem does it while you can still act. Research on 'prospective hindsight' found that imagining an event has already happened helps people come up with more reasons for it (Mitchell, Russo & Pennington, 1989).
cards.model: Pretend it already failed, then ask why. Fix those reasons before you start.
cards.try_today: Take one plan for this week. Spend 3 minutes writing 'It failed because…' five times. Fix the easiest one now.

source.work: Back to the Future: Temporal Perspective in the Explanation of Events (1989); Performing a Project Premortem (Harvard Business Review, 2007)

cards.hook: Coin flip: win $100 or lose $40. On average, what's a flip worth?
cards.title: Expected Value

game.question: Heads you win $100, tails you lose $40. On average, how much is one flip worth?
game.explain: Expected value = chance × payoff, added up. 0.5 × $100 + 0.5 × (−$40) = $50 − $20 = $30. Over many flips, you'd average about $30 a flip.

cards.insight: Losses tend to feel about twice as strong as equal gains (loss aversion), so some people still hesitate here. Expected value shows the math under the feeling. One flip can still lose, so only bet what you can afford to lose.
cards.model: Odds × payoff, added up. Take bets with positive value that you can afford to lose.
cards.try_today: Write two outcomes for one choice today, each with a rough chance and payoff. Multiply each pair and compare.

source.work: Pascal–Fermat letters (1654); Prospect Theory (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979); Thinking in Bets (2018)

cards.hook: Bad outcome = bad decision? That one rule can quietly wreck you.
cards.title: Judge the Decision, Not the Dice

steps.scenario: Your friend researched a job offer for weeks, talked to staff, checked the company's finances. Six months later, the company shuts down. They say: 'I'm so stupid for taking it.' You reply…

options.text: "You decided well with what you knew. The outcome was bad luck."
options.feedback: Yes. Separating decision quality from outcome is the whole skill. It keeps them learning instead of blaming.

options.text: "Yeah, you should have seen it coming."
options.feedback: Hindsight makes the future look obvious. If no info pointed to it, the decision wasn't the problem.

options.text: "Never trust a job offer again."
options.feedback: Understandable instinct, but it learns the wrong lesson from one roll of the dice.

steps.scenario: Now flip it. Someone drives home after drinking and arrives safely. Good decision?

options.text: No. A good outcome doesn't fix a bad bet.
options.feedback: Right. The risk was real; they just got lucky. Luck doesn't make the decision wise.

options.text: Yes, nothing bad happened.
options.feedback: That's 'resulting': grading a choice by how it turned out. It teaches people to repeat lucky mistakes.

cards.insight: Poker player Annie Duke calls it 'resulting': judging a decision only by its outcome. Life has luck in it. Good choices sometimes lose and bad ones sometimes win. Judge yourself on the process, and you'll learn the right lessons.
cards.model: Decision quality = what you knew and how you weighed it. Outcome = decision + luck.
cards.try_today: Pick one past choice you regret. Ask: given what I knew then, was it reasonable? Write one sentence answering.

source.work: Thinking in Bets (2018)

cards.hook: Saying 'yes' to this costs more than its price tag. Want to see?
cards.title: Opportunity Cost

game.prompt: A movie you like costs $14.99. Option A: buy it. Option B: keep the $14.99 for other things you want. Which do you pick?
game.reveal: In one study, 75% bought when the options were 'buy' or 'don't buy'. Adding 'keep the $14.99 for other purchases' dropped buyers to 55% (Frederick et al., 2009). Later replications found the effect, but often smaller.

cards.insight: Every yes is a no to something else: money, time, attention. Our minds rarely show us the thing we're giving up unless someone says it out loud. Economist Frédéric Bastiat called it 'what is not seen'.
cards.model: The real price of a yes is the best thing it pushes out. Name it before you agree.
cards.try_today: Name what you're giving up before your next yes (a purchase, a meeting, an hour online). Then decide.

source.work: What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen (1850); Opportunity Cost Neglect (Journal of Consumer Research, 2009)

cards.hook: Pick one topic you give advice on. Are you inside your circle?
cards.title: Circle of Competence

questions.q: Think of one topic you give advice on. I've had real results in it, not just opinions.
I can explain where my knowledge on it stops.
People who know more than me would mostly agree with my advice.
I feel sure when I talk about it.
I'd make a big decision on it without asking anyone.
I often say 'I'm not sure' on this topic.

results.name: The Explorer
results.text: You're early on this topic and you know it. That's honest. Learn by asking people inside their circle, and keep decisions small and reversible for now.

C.name: Edge Walker
C.text: Your confidence is ahead of your track record. That's where mistakes live. Before big calls, ask someone with results to check you.

K.name: Quiet Expert
K.text: You know more than you claim. Humility is good, but your knowledge could help others. Share it, and note where it ends.

CK.name: Inside the Circle
CK.text: Confidence and proof line up. Great. Your job now is guarding the border: notice when a question drifts outside what you've tested.

cards.insight: Warren Buffett's rule: the size of your circle matters less than knowing where its edge is. Socrates made the same point 2,400 years ago: wisdom starts with knowing what you don't know. Trouble comes when confidence spreads wider than real knowledge.
cards.model: Know the edge of what you know. Act boldly inside it; ask, test, or pass outside it.
cards.try_today: Write one topic where you're truly competent and one where you only feel confident. Ask an expert one question on the second.

source.work: Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letter (1996); Plato, Apology

cards.hook: You say you feel 'bad'. Can you do anything with that word?
cards.title: Name It to Tame It

game.prompt: Could you act on this feeling-word?

items.text: "I feel bad."
items.why: Bad how? Sad, guilty, tired, scared? Each one needs a different fix.

items.text: "I'm embarrassed about the meeting and also just tired."
items.why: Two clear parts: one needs a quick repair, the other needs sleep.

items.text: "Ugh. Everything."
items.why: 'Everything' is too big to touch. Shrink it to one feeling, one cause.

items.text: "I'm anxious because I haven't opened the bill yet."
items.why: Now the next step is obvious: open the bill.

items.text: "I'm stressed."
items.why: Stressed could be overloaded, unsure, or lonely. Dig one layer down.

items.text: "I feel left out because nobody replied in the group chat."
items.why: Specific feeling plus cause. You can check the story or reach out.

cards.insight: Precise feelings come with handles; vague ones don't. People who tell their emotions apart in finer detail tend to cope better with stress. Lisa Feldman Barrett calls this emotional granularity.
cards.model: A vague feeling is a fog. A named feeling is a map with a next step on it.
cards.try_today: Next time you think 'I feel bad', swap it for two exact words, like 'disappointed and hungry'. Then act on the easier one.

source.work: How Emotions Are Made (2017); Kashdan, Barrett & McKnight, 'Unpacking Emotion Differentiation' (2015)

cards.hook: Saying 'I'm angry' out loud: does it fuel the anger or cool it?
cards.title: The Label Effect

game.prompt: In a brain-scan study, people looked at angry and scared faces. Some just matched the faces. Others picked a word for the emotion, like 'angry'. What happened in the alarm center of their brain?
choices: Naming it made the alarm louder
game.reveal: Naming it calmed it. Choosing the emotion word reduced activity in the amygdala, the brain's alarm, compared with just matching faces (Lieberman et al., 2007). Putting feelings into words seems to turn the volume down a little.

cards.insight: Naming a feeling doesn't feed it; it gives your thinking brain a job. It won't erase the feeling, but it can take the edge off enough for you to choose what to do next.
cards.model: Words are a dimmer switch for feelings: name it and the alarm quiets down.
cards.try_today: When something stings today, finish this sentence in your head or in a note: 'Right now I feel ___ because ___.'

source.work: Lieberman et al., 'Putting Feelings Into Words', Psychological Science (2007)

cards.hook: You fired off that reply in 4 seconds. Where did your choice go?
cards.title: The Pause

game.prompt: Put the pause back in order, from trigger to response
items: Trigger: the message lands
Notice the body: hot face, tight chest
Name it: 'I feel disrespected'
Breathe: three slow breaths, long exhales
Choose: reply now, later, or not at all
game.explain: Most regretted reactions skip straight from step 1 to step 5. Each middle step adds a few seconds, and those seconds are where your options appear.

cards.insight: A reaction is fast and automatic. A response is a reaction with a few seconds of thinking added. You can't stop the first jolt, but you can stretch the gap before you act. (The famous 'space between stimulus and response' quote is often credited to Viktor Frankl, but it isn't found in his books.)
cards.model: Feel it fast, act on it slow. The pause is where your choice lives.
cards.try_today: Before your next heated reply, take three slow breaths with longer exhales than inhales, then decide: now, later, or never.

source.work: Emotional Intelligence (1995)

cards.hook: Your boss emails 'We need to talk.' at 9pm. Your move?
cards.title: Pause Before Send

steps.scenario: 9:04pm. An email from your manager: 'We need to talk tomorrow.' Your stomach drops. You…

options.text: Reply right away: 'Is something wrong?? I can explain whatever it is.'
options.feedback: Totally human: the worry wants an answer now. But replying from panic often adds stress for both of you.

options.text: Notice the dread, name it ('I'm scared I messed up'), and breathe before doing anything.
options.feedback: Yes. You felt the jolt and didn't let it drive. Naming the fear already shrinks it a little.

options.text: Spend two hours imagining every way you might be fired.
options.feedback: Your brain is trying to protect you by rehearsing threats. It rarely helps, and it costs sleep.

steps.scenario: You've paused. The worry is still there. What now?

options.text: Send a short, calm reply ('Sure, what time works?') or decide to answer in the morning. Then close the laptop.
options.feedback: Calm, clear, done. Either way you made a choice, and you're responding to the email, not the worst story about it.

options.text: Write a long defensive message listing everything you did well this month.
options.feedback: Understandable, but you're answering an accusation nobody made yet. Save it for the actual talk if needed.

options.text: Keep rereading the email in bed, trying to decode a hidden meaning.
options.feedback: Very common. But the email holds no more information than before, so rereading mostly feeds the worry and costs sleep.

cards.insight: A vague message plus a tired brain at night is a recipe for worst-case stories. The pause doesn't remove the worry; it keeps the worry from writing your reply. Most 'we need to talk' messages turn out more ordinary than the story you built.
cards.model: Respond to what was said, not to the scariest story your brain wrote about it.
cards.try_today: Pick one message you're tempted to answer instantly today. Wait 10 minutes, reread it, then reply.

source.work: Emotional Intelligence (1995); Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011)

cards.hook: Would you talk to a friend the way you talked to yourself today?
cards.title: Inner Critic or Inner Coach?

questions.q: You make a dumb mistake at work. Your first inner words are…

options.label: 'Oops. Anyone could do that. What's the fix?'

questions.q: You're struggling and others seem fine. You think…

options.label: 'Lots of people struggle with this, even if they don't show it.'

questions.q: When you feel low, you tend to…

options.label: Notice it and ask what you need right now

questions.q: Being kind to yourself after failing feels like…

zones.label: Critic-leaning
zones.text: Your inner voice is tough on you, often because it wants to keep you safe or improving. You can keep the high standards and drop the insults. Try speaking to yourself like a good coach would.

zones.label: Mixed
zones.text: You swing between harsh and fair. Notice which situations flip the critic on, so you can catch it sooner.

zones.label: Coach-leaning
zones.text: You tend to meet setbacks with kindness and a plan. That's a skill, not softness. Keep it, especially on bad days.

cards.insight: Kristin Neff describes self-compassion as kindness to yourself, remembering everyone struggles, and seeing pain clearly without drowning in it. It isn't letting yourself off: in one study, people prompted to be self-compassionate after failing a test chose to study longer for the retest.
cards.model: High standards, kind voice. Coaches correct mistakes without insulting the player.
cards.try_today: Write one sentence to yourself about a recent mistake, exactly as you'd write it to a friend who made the same one.

source.work: Neff, 'Self-Compassion' (2003); Breines & Chen, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin (2012)

cards.hook: You put it off again. Guilt or forgiveness: which gets it done?
cards.title: Procrastination Is a Feeling Problem

game.prompt: Students who procrastinated studying for a first exam were later asked how much they had forgiven themselves for it. Before the next exam, who procrastinated less?
choices: Those who stayed hard on themselves
game.reveal: The ones who forgave themselves procrastinated less the next time (Wohl, Pychyl & Bennett, 2010). It was one correlational study, not proof, but it fits the idea: guilt keeps the task linked to a bad feeling, and we avoid bad feelings.

cards.insight: We rarely avoid the task itself. We avoid the feeling it gives us: boredom, confusion, fear of doing it badly. Delay is a quick mood fix that costs you later. Beating yourself up adds more bad feeling to the same task, so it often backfires.
cards.model: You're not avoiding the task. You're avoiding a feeling. Shrink the feeling and the task gets easier to start.
cards.try_today: Name the feeling the task gives you, forgive yesterday's delay in one sentence, then work on it for just 5 minutes.

source.work: Wohl, Pychyl & Bennett, Personality and Individual Differences (2010); Sirois & Pychyl (2013)

cards.hook: Can a news feed change your mood? Guess how many got tested.
cards.title: Moods Are Contagious

game.question: In 2012, Facebook quietly showed fewer happy or fewer sad posts to some users to see if moods spread. How many people were in the study?
game.explain: 689,003 users, for one week (Kramer, Guillory & Hancock, 2014). People who saw fewer positive posts wrote slightly fewer positive words themselves, and the reverse held too. It measured words, not felt mood, the effect was tiny, and users never agreed to take part.

cards.insight: Moods spread between people through faces, voices and even text. The online effect in this study was very small per person, but small nudges add up across a whole day of scrolling and a whole room of people. You catch moods, and you also give them off.
cards.model: Moods are weather. Notice what front you walked into, and what front you bring with you.
cards.try_today: Before your next meeting, call, or group chat, take one breath and pick the mood you want to bring into it.

source.work: Hatfield, Cacioppo & Rapson, Emotional Contagion (1994); Kramer et al., PNAS (2014)

cards.hook: When something's hard, what's the first sentence in your head?
cards.title: Fixed vs Growth Mindset

questions.q: You bomb a test in a new subject. Your first thought is…

options.label: I'm just not a numbers person.
Ugh. Maybe I'm not cut out for this.
My method didn't work. Time for a new one.

questions.q: A friend is way better than you at something you care about.

options.label: They're a natural. I'll never catch up.
I'd rather not compare, it stings.

questions.q: Someone gives you blunt feedback on your work.

options.label: It feels like a verdict on me.
I get defensive first, then think.
It's free information about the work.

questions.q: Picking between an easy task and a stretch task, you usually…

options.label: Take the easy one. Why risk looking bad?
Take the stretch. That's where I grow.

zones.label: Fixed-leaning
zones.text: Hard things feel like tests of who you are. That's tiring. Try treating the next one as a test of your method instead.

zones.label: Mixed (like most people)
zones.text: Everyone carries both mindsets. Notice which topics flip you to 'fixed', that's where the work is.

zones.label: Growth-leaning
zones.text: You treat ability as trainable. Pair that with real strategy changes, not just 'try harder', and it pays off.

cards.insight: Your mindset isn't one setting: it shifts by topic. Big studies find teaching a growth mindset helps a little on average, mostly for students who are struggling. It's a useful lens, not magic.
cards.model: Treat a struggle as feedback on your method, not a verdict on your worth.
cards.try_today: Pick one 'I'm just not a ___ person' belief and write one different method you haven't tried yet.

source.work: Mindset: The New Psychology of Success (2006)

cards.hook: One kind of compliment may nudge kids to dodge hard problems. Which?
cards.title: Praise the Process

steps.scenario: Your 11-year-old cousin aces a tricky maths quiz and shows you, beaming. You say…

options.text: "Wow, you're so smart!"
options.feedback: Totally natural and kind. The catch: if 'smart' is the reason, a future hard problem can feel like proof they aren't.

options.text: "Nice! What did you do to crack the hard ones?"
options.feedback: This points at what they did, something they can repeat next time. It also gets them talking.

options.text: "Cool, but was it an easy quiz?"
options.feedback: Probably meant as a joke, but it shrinks the win. Celebrate first, calibrate later.

steps.scenario: Next week they fail a quiz and say, "I'm just bad at maths." You reply…

options.text: "No you're not, you're brilliant!"
options.feedback: Warm, but it argues with their feeling and gives them nothing to do next.

options.text: "Not everyone's a maths person, it's fine."
options.feedback: Kind intent, but it confirms the fixed story they just told themselves.

options.text: "This topic isn't clicking yet. What did you try? What could you try next?"
options.feedback: Accepts the feeling, adds 'yet', and turns it into a plan. That's the growth move.

cards.insight: In a classic 1998 study, kids praised for being smart later chose easier tasks than kids praised for effort. Replications are mixed and effects small, but praising strategy is low-risk and gives people something to repeat.
cards.model: Praise what someone did (strategy, effort, choices), not what they are.
cards.try_today: Give one person a compliment today that names a specific thing they did, not a trait they have.

source.work: Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance (1998)

cards.hook: What if your report card said 'Not Yet' instead of 'Fail'?
cards.title: The Power of 'Yet'

game.prompt: You get a result back. Box A says 'FAIL'. Box B says 'NOT YET'. Same score. Which one makes you more likely to try again?
game.reveal: Carol Dweck tells of a Chicago high school that graded unfinished courses 'Not Yet'. It's a story, not a study, but the point stands: 'Fail' sounds like an ending, 'Not yet' sounds like a road.

cards.insight: Adding 'yet' doesn't change your skill, it changes the story about time. 'I can't' sounds permanent. 'I can't yet' says you're on a path, which makes the next attempt feel worth making.
cards.model: Add 'yet': it turns a verdict into a stage on a path.
cards.try_today: Catch one 'I can't…' you say today and finish it out loud with '…yet, and my next step is ___'.

source.work: The Power of Believing That You Can Improve, TED talk (2014)

cards.hook: West Point's toughest summer: who made it through?
cards.title: Grit vs Talent

game.prompt: New West Point cadets face 'Beast Barracks', a brutal first summer. The academy scores every cadet on grades, fitness and leadership. What better predicted who stayed?
game.reveal: In a 2007 study, a short grit survey predicted who finished Beast Barracks better than the academy's own score. But dropouts were rare, and later reviews found grit overlaps heavily with conscientiousness and predicts less than first claimed.

cards.insight: Sticking with one goal through boredom and setbacks matters. But grit is contested: a 2017 meta-analysis of 88 samples found its links to success modest, mostly from the perseverance part. Treat it as one ingredient, not the recipe.
cards.model: Talent and staying power both count; neither alone is the whole story.
cards.try_today: Name one long-term goal and write the single smallest action that keeps it alive this week.

source.work: Grit: Perseverance and passion for long-term goals (2007); Much ado about grit (2017)

cards.hook: Are you a sprinter, a wanderer, or a long-haul builder?
cards.title: Your Grit Map

questions.q: I've cared about the same big goal for over a year.
New ideas often pull me away from old projects.
I know what I'm working toward in the next few years.
Setbacks don't knock me off course for long.
I usually lose steam after the first few weeks.
I finish what I start, even the boring parts.

results.name: The Explorer
results.text: You're still sampling, and that's valid: interests are often found by trying things. Pick one thread to follow for a month and see if it holds.

P.name: The Dreamer
P.text: You know what lights you up, but effort comes in bursts. Shrink the daily step so small you can't skip it.

S.name: The Workhorse
S.text: You can grind. Check that you're grinding toward something you actually chose, not just what's in front of you.

PS.name: The Long-Haul Builder
PS.text: Stable interest plus staying power. Protect it by also knowing when a path stops serving you: grit includes smart quitting.

cards.insight: Duckworth splits grit into two parts: keeping the same interest over time, and pushing through setbacks. How much grit predicts success is debated, so treat this as a mirror, not a score. Build the half that's weaker.
cards.model: Grit = a direction you keep + effort you sustain. Build the weaker half.
cards.try_today: Write your one-sentence 'top goal' on a sticky note and put it where you'll see it tomorrow morning.

source.work: Grit: The Power of Passion and Perseverance (2016)

cards.hook: Played guitar for 10 years? Why might you be no better than year 2?
cards.title: Deliberate Practice

game.prompt: Put the deliberate practice loop in order
items: Pick one specific weakness
Set a goal just past your current ability
Practise with full focus
Get immediate feedback
Adjust and repeat
game.explain: Comfortable repetition keeps you where you are. Improvement comes from aiming at one weak spot, just beyond your reach, with fast feedback telling you what to change.

cards.insight: Hours alone don't make experts; focused practice on weak spots helps far more. The '10,000-hour rule' (popularised by Gladwell) oversimplifies Ericsson's work, and a 2014 meta-analysis found practice explains only part of skill differences.
cards.model: Not more practice: harder, narrower practice with feedback.
cards.try_today: Pick a skill you use often, name its weakest sub-part, and drill only that for 10 focused minutes.

source.work: Peak (2016); Deliberate practice and performance: a meta-analysis (2014)

cards.hook: You just messed up at work. What you do in the next hour matters.
cards.title: Mistakes as Data

steps.scenario: You sent a report with a wrong number to your whole team. Someone points it out. Your first move…

options.text: Quietly fix it and hope nobody else noticed.
options.feedback: Very human. But the lesson stays hidden, and others may still be using the wrong number.

options.text: Send a short correction: what was wrong, the right number, done.
options.feedback: Clean and calm. Owning it fast builds trust and stops the error spreading.

options.text: Apologise at length about how careless you are.
options.feedback: Harsh self-talk feels responsible but uses energy you need for the fix. Be kind to yourself and precise about the error.

steps.scenario: That evening the mistake is still on your mind. What do you do with it?

options.text: Replay it and feel bad until it fades.
options.feedback: Understandable, but feeling bad isn't the same as learning. The pain is a signal, not the lesson.

options.text: Write 3 lines: what happened, why, what I'll change.
options.feedback: This is the alchemy: a mistake turned into a rule you keep, like 'double-check numbers before sending'.

options.text: Decide you're not cut out for this job.
options.feedback: One error is one data point, not a verdict on you. Look for the cause you can change.

cards.insight: A mistake shows exactly where your method breaks, more precisely than any praise. Ray Dalio sums it up as pain plus reflection equals progress. The trick is reflecting on the cause, not punishing yourself.
cards.model: Mistake → cause → new rule. Keep the lesson, drop the shame.
cards.try_today: Write down one recent mistake in 3 lines: what happened, why, and one rule you'll follow next time.

source.work: Principles: Life and Work (2017)

cards.hook: Managers ranked 5 motivators. Guess where 'progress' landed.
cards.title: The Cookie Jar of Wins

game.question: 669 managers ranked five workplace motivators (like recognition, incentives, clear goals, support, and making progress). Where did 'making progress' land? (1 = top, 5 = last)
game.explain: Dead last. Yet in nearly 12,000 diary entries from 238 knowledge workers, making progress on meaningful work was the strongest booster of their best days.

cards.insight: We underrate small steps forward, even though diary studies show they lift motivation most. David Goggins calls it a 'cookie jar': a mental store of past wins you reach into when things get hard. Small wins become fuel.
cards.model: Progress you can see is the strongest fuel. Keep evidence of it.
cards.try_today: Start a 'cookie jar' note: list 3 hard things you've already handled. Add one small win every evening.

source.work: The Progress Principle (2011); Can't Hurt Me (2018)

cards.hook: Is this the dip you push through, or the sign to walk away?
cards.title: Quitting Wisely

game.prompt: Quit signal or push through?

items.text: It's hard, but you're measurably better than a month ago.
items.why: Hard plus progress is the classic dip. That's where the reward usually lies beyond.

items.text: You keep going mainly because of what you've already spent.
items.why: That's the sunk cost trap. Past costs are gone either way; judge only the road ahead.

items.text: Knowing what you know now, you'd never start this today.
items.why: Annie Duke's test: if you wouldn't choose it fresh, staying is often just inertia.

items.text: You had a terrible week and feel like giving up tonight.
items.why: Don't decide on your worst day. Rest, then set a calm review date and decide then.

items.text: Your goal changed and this no longer leads anywhere you want.
items.why: Grit toward the wrong goal is just stubbornness. Redirect the effort.

items.text: It keeps costing you sleep, health, or key relationships.
items.why: Real harm is a stop sign, not a toughness test. Protect the base everything else is built on.

items.text: You're stuck, but you haven't tried a new method yet.
items.why: Change the approach before you change the goal. Stuck is often a method problem.

cards.insight: Quitting isn't failure; it frees time and energy for better bets. Seth Godin separates 'the dip' worth pushing through from dead ends. Annie Duke adds: we usually quit too late, held back by sunk costs.
cards.model: Quit what you wouldn't start today. Push through dips that still show progress.
cards.try_today: Write one commitment you're unsure about and set a 'kill criteria': the signal that would tell you to stop.

source.work: Quit (2022); The Dip (2007)

cards.hook: Your phone buzzes and your hand moves first. What just happened?
cards.title: The Habit Loop

game.prompt: You check your phone without deciding to. Put the loop in order.
items: Cue: the buzz
Craving: what's new?
Response: you unlock it
Reward: a small hit of novelty
game.explain: This is James Clear's four-step version; Duhigg's original had three (cue, routine, reward). The cue triggers a craving, the craving drives a response, and the reward teaches your brain to repeat it next time.

cards.insight: Habits are not character flaws. They are shortcuts your brain automated to save effort. You don't have to beat the whole loop. Change one link (hide the cue, swap the response) and the loop starts to change.
cards.model: Cue, craving, response, reward. Break or rebuild any single link to change the habit.
cards.try_today: Pick one habit you want to change and write its cue on paper. Just noticing the trigger is step one.

source.work: The Power of Habit (2012); Atomic Habits (2018)

cards.hook: How long until a new habit runs on autopilot? Not 21 days.
cards.title: How Long a Habit Really Takes

game.question: In a UK study, people built one new daily habit. How many days did it take, on median, to feel automatic?
game.explain: Lally and colleagues (2010) followed 96 people and found a median of 66 days, with a huge estimated range: 18 to 254 days. The popular '21 days' figure has no solid research behind it.

cards.insight: If a habit still feels effortful after three weeks, you're not failing. You're normal. Simple habits (a glass of water) automate faster than hard ones (50 sit-ups). Patience is part of the method.
cards.model: Habits take about two months on average, and the range is wide. Plan for the long middle.
cards.try_today: Pick one tiny habit and mark a date 66 days from today in your calendar as its check-in day.

source.work: How are habits formed (European Journal of Social Psychology, 2010)

cards.hook: Are you chasing a goal, or becoming someone? Your words reveal it.
cards.title: Outcome vs Identity Habits

questions.q: Someone offers you something you're cutting back on (a cigarette, a sugary snack). You say...

options.label: No thanks, I'm trying to quit.
No thanks, that's not really me anymore.

questions.q: Your fitness aim sounds most like...

options.label: Be someone who moves every day.

questions.q: After a good workout you think...

options.label: One step closer to the target.
That's the kind of person I am.

questions.q: When you skip a day you think...

options.label: Back at it tomorrow, it's who I am.

zones.label: Outcome-leaning
zones.text: You aim at results. Useful for direction, but results take time and you may feel stuck before they show. Try adding a 'who am I becoming' line.

zones.label: Mixed
zones.text: You use both. Goals set the direction; identity keeps you going when results are slow.

zones.label: Identity-leaning
zones.text: You tie actions to who you are. That makes habits sticky. Just keep the identity flexible so one slip doesn't feel like a verdict.

cards.insight: Goals tell you where to go; identity decides whether you keep going. Each small action is a vote for a type of person. You don't need a unanimous vote, just a majority over time.
cards.model: Every action is a vote for the person you're becoming. Win the majority, not every vote.
cards.try_today: Finish this sentence on paper: 'I am the kind of person who...' Then do one 2-minute action that proves it.

source.work: Atomic Habits (2018)

cards.hook: One word seemed to get more people voting. Can you guess which?
cards.title: Be a Voter, Not Just Vote

game.prompt: Before an election, researchers asked people one of two questions. Which version got more people to actually vote?
choices: How important is it to you to vote?
How important is it to you to be a voter?
game.reveal: In Bryan and colleagues' 2011 study, the 'be a voter' wording raised turnout. Later, larger studies (Gerber et al., 2016) did not find the same effect, so treat this as a promising idea, not a law.

cards.insight: Framing an action as part of who you are ('a voter', 'a reader') may make it feel more meaningful. The evidence is mixed: the original finding did not reliably replicate. Still, it costs nothing to describe yourself kindly and specifically.
cards.model: Nouns can pull harder than verbs: 'I'm a reader' may stick better than 'I should read'. Evidence is mixed.
