cards.try_today: Rename one goal as a noun: change 'I should run' to 'I'm a runner', then do the smallest version of it today.

source.work: Motivating voter turnout by invoking the self (PNAS, 2011)

cards.hook: Get 1% better every day for a year. Guess how much better you are.
cards.title: 1% Compounding

game.question: If you improve 1% every day for 365 days, how many times better are you at the end?
game.explain: 1.01 to the power of 365 is about 37.8. The flip side: getting 1% worse daily (0.99^365) leaves you at about 0.03, nearly zero. Growth like this feels slow at first because we tend to think in straight lines.

cards.insight: Our brains expect straight-line progress, so small daily gains feel pointless at first. Real life isn't this tidy (skills plateau, days vary), so take this as an illustration, not a forecast. The point stands: small, repeated choices add up in both directions.
cards.model: Tiny gains compound. Judge your habits by their direction, not by today's result.
cards.try_today: Pick one thing you do daily and make it 1% better today: one more page, one less scroll, one extra glass of water.

source.work: Atomic Habits (2018)

cards.hook: Your habit is too big to start. Can you shrink it to two minutes?
cards.title: The Two-Minute Rule

game.prompt: Is this a good two-minute starting version?

items.text: Read one page of a book
items.why: Tiny, clear, and it often turns into more pages.

items.text: Read 30 pages every night
items.why: Great goal, hard start. Shrink it to one page first.

items.text: Put on your running shoes
items.why: Starting is the hard part. Shoes on makes the run likely.

items.text: Run 5 km before work
items.why: Make the first step the shoes, not the whole run.

items.text: Write one sentence in a journal
items.why: One sentence is easy to say yes to, even on bad days.

items.text: Clean the whole flat
items.why: Try 'put away one thing' instead. Momentum does the rest.

cards.insight: For many people, starting is the hardest part. Shrink the habit until it's almost silly, and the start stops being a battle. This is a practical rule of thumb, not a lab finding. Clear adapted it from David Allen's rule: if a task takes under two minutes, do it now.
cards.model: Make the start so small you can't say no. Master showing up before you improve.
cards.try_today: Take one habit you keep postponing and do only its two-minute version right now. Stopping after is allowed.

source.work: Atomic Habits (2018); Getting Things Done (2001); Tiny Habits (2019)

cards.hook: People with 'great willpower' may just face fewer temptations. You?
cards.title: Design the Room, Not the Will

questions.q: The things I want to do more (book, water, guitar) are in plain sight.
Starting a good habit takes me under 20 seconds of setup.
Temptations (snacks, games) take effort to reach.
My phone is out of reach when I need to focus or sleep.
My default options (what's on my plate, my home screen) are good ones.
The people I spend time with do the habits I want.

advice.0: Make good cues visible: put the book on your pillow or the water bottle on your desk.
advice.1: Add friction to temptations and remove it from good habits: lay out tomorrow's gym clothes tonight.
advice.2: Charge your phone outside the bedroom tonight, or in another room while you work.
advice.3: Change one default: move social apps off your home screen, or put fruit at eye level.
advice.4: Find one person or group who already does the habit you want, and spend a little time there.

cards.insight: In one study, people who rated their self-control highly reported meeting fewer temptations, not resisting more (Hofmann et al., 2012). In-the-moment willpower is hard work to rely on. Your surroundings work every day for free.
cards.model: Make good habits obvious and easy; make bad ones invisible and hard.
cards.try_today: Move one temptation out of sight and put one good cue in plain view. It takes two minutes.

source.work: Atomic Habits (2018); Everyday temptations (J. Personality & Social Psychology, 2012); Good Habits, Bad Habits (2019)

cards.hook: You broke your streak yesterday. What you do next matters more.
cards.title: Never Miss Twice

steps.scenario: You've walked every evening for 12 days. Yesterday you were exhausted and skipped. Tonight you...

options.text: Do a 5-minute walk, even if it's short.
options.feedback: Yes. A small rep tonight keeps the habit alive. Getting back quickly matters more than the perfect streak.

options.text: Wait until Monday to restart properly.
options.feedback: Understandable, but waiting turns one miss into a new pattern. A small walk tonight works better.

options.text: Decide you're just not a walking person.
options.feedback: That's a big verdict from one tired day. One miss says nothing about who you are.

steps.scenario: A friend says: 'I missed my workout, so the week is ruined.' You reply...

options.text: Missing once barely matters. What's the smallest workout you could do today?
options.feedback: Kind and practical. You lowered the shame and the bar at the same time.

options.text: You need more discipline.
options.feedback: Well meant, but shame tends to make restarting harder, not easier.

options.text: Yeah, just start fresh next week.
options.feedback: Supportive, but it delays the comeback. Today is a fine day to restart.

cards.insight: In Lally's 2010 habit study, missing a single day did not meaningfully slow habit formation. What hurts is the slide: 'I've already blown it' becomes a week off. Treat a miss as an accident, not a verdict, and come back small.
cards.model: Missing once is an accident. Missing twice risks starting a new pattern. Return small and fast.
cards.try_today: If you missed something this week, do a tiny version of it today and tell yourself: 'One miss doesn't define me.'

source.work: Atomic Habits (2018); How are habits formed (2010)

cards.hook: You get 10 seconds to recruit a stranger. What do you say first?
cards.title: Lead With the Why

steps.scenario: You're starting a Saturday park clean-up and need volunteers. A neighbour stops to listen. Your first sentence is…

options.text: "We meet at 9, bring gloves, it takes two hours."
options.feedback: Useful details, but they answer a question nobody has asked yet. Logistics land better once people care.

options.text: "Kids can't play in that park because of broken glass. I want to fix that."
options.feedback: You gave a reason they can feel. Now the time and the gloves sound like a way to help, not a chore.

options.text: "We're the biggest clean-up group in the area."
options.feedback: Size can impress, but it's about you. People join for what it means to them.

steps.scenario: They say: "Sounds good, but I'm busy." You reply…

options.text: "Even 30 minutes helps. The playground corner is the worst bit."
options.feedback: You kept the why alive and made the ask smaller. Easy yes, no pressure.

options.text: "Everyone's busy. It's only two hours."
options.feedback: Understandable, but it brushes off their reason. People dig in when they feel unheard.

options.text: "No worries." and walk off.
options.feedback: Kind and respectful. You could also leave a door open with a smaller, clear option.

cards.insight: When you opened with the reason, the details started to sound like an invitation. Sinek's 'Golden Circle' says lead with why, then how, then what. The habit is useful, but his brain-biology explanation is contested and not backed by neuroscience.
cards.model: Say why it matters before what it is. Purpose first, logistics second.
cards.try_today: Before your next request or pitch, write one sentence that starts with "This matters because…" and say that first.

source.work: Start With Why (2009)

cards.hook: Which week would you call more meaningful: easy or heavy?
cards.title: Meaning Lives in the Load

game.prompt: Week A: lie-ins, good food, nothing asked of you. Week B: tiring, but you helped a friend move and finished something people rely on. Which one would you call more meaningful?
game.reveal: Many people pick Week B as more meaningful, even if Week A felt happier. A 2013 survey study by Baumeister and colleagues found happiness linked more to getting what you want, and meaning linked more to giving, caring for others and facing hard things. Frankl argued something similar from his own life.

cards.insight: Happiness and meaning overlap, but they aren't the same. Meaning tends to grow where you carry something for someone. That doesn't mean piling on until you break. It means choosing a load that is truly yours and worth carrying.
cards.model: Happiness is often about receiving; meaning is often about carrying something worth it.
cards.try_today: Pick one small thing someone relies on you for and do it a little better than needed today, on purpose.

source.work: Man's Search for Meaning (1946); Baumeister et al., Journal of Positive Psychology (2013)

cards.hook: Not every weight is yours. Can you tell which ones are?
cards.title: Pick Up the Right Load

game.prompt: Is this a load you can pick up today?

items.text: How you show up for the people who count on you
items.why: Your reliability is fully yours. It's where meaning starts.

items.text: Making everyone at work like you
items.why: Their feelings aren't yours to control. Your fairness and effort are.

items.text: The mess in your room that's been bugging you
items.why: Small, concrete, yours. Sorting it is a quick win that steadies you.

items.text: Fixing a friend's life for them
items.why: You can support them. Taking over their choices is a weight that crushes both of you.

items.text: Learning the skill your goal actually needs
items.why: Closing your own skill gap is a load that pays you back.

items.text: Every bad thing in the news today
items.why: Caring is good. Carrying it all is not. Pick one thing you can act on instead.

cards.insight: Meaning comes from responsibility, but only the kind you can actually act on. Loads that are truly yours make you stronger. Loads that belong to others, or to the whole world, mostly bring worry. Sorting them is the first step.
cards.model: Carry what's yours, fully. Put down what isn't, kindly.
cards.try_today: Write down three things weighing on you. Circle the one you can act on, and take one 5-minute step on it.

source.work: 12 Rules for Life (2018); Enchiridion (c. 125 AD)

cards.hook: Is your life a cage or a flood right now? Find your spot.
cards.title: The Border of Order & Chaos

questions.q: My typical week is…

options.label: Different every day, hard to plan

questions.q: When did you last learn something genuinely new?
When a plan changes last minute, I feel…

options.label: Annoyed, I like it how it was
Relieved, plans were never real anyway

questions.q: My sleep, meals and money are…

zones.label: Leaning Order
zones.text: Safe and predictable, but it may be getting a bit tight. Add one small unknown: a new route, a new skill, a new person.

zones.label: On the Border
zones.text: You've got enough structure to stand on and enough novelty to grow. That's the sweet spot. Keep it.

zones.label: Leaning Chaos
zones.text: Lots is moving. One fixed anchor helps: same wake time, one daily walk, or a weekly money check.

cards.insight: Too much order and life goes stale. Too much chaos and you can't find your footing. Taoist thought pictures opposites like these as partners, and Peterson says meaning is found on the border between them. It's a lens, not a law: the right mix shifts over your life.
cards.model: Stand on order, step into chaos. Growth happens at the edge between them.
cards.try_today: If you lean Order, try one new thing today. If you lean Chaos, fix one anchor: same bedtime tonight.

source.work: Tao Te Ching (c. 4th century BC); Maps of Meaning (1999); 12 Rules for Life (2018)

cards.hook: A gorilla walks through a video. Would you even notice it?
cards.title: Your Aim Decides What You See

game.prompt: You watch a short clip and count how many times players in white pass a basketball. Halfway through, a person in a gorilla suit walks across the screen. Would you notice?
game.reveal: In Simons and Chabris's 1999 study, about half of viewers missed the gorilla. Their aim (count the passes) filtered out everything else. Your goals act like a spotlight: you see what serves them and miss the rest.

cards.insight: In the study, the counting task filtered out the gorilla. That part is solid science. The life lesson is a lens, not a proven law: your aims shape what you notice, so a clear, worthy aim can help you spot chances, people and tools you'd otherwise miss.
cards.model: What you aim at shapes what you see. Choose the aim on purpose.
cards.try_today: Write one aim for this week in a single line. Tonight, list three things you noticed today that could help it.

source.work: Gorillas in our midst, Perception (1999); Nicomachean Ethics; 12 Rules for Life (2018)

cards.hook: Bored, stressed, or lost in it? Watch your dot find the zone.
cards.title: Find Your Flow Channel

questions.q: Think of your main task this week. It stretches me.
I could do it half-asleep.
There's a real chance I'll fall short.
I know how to do most of it well.
I often feel lost about where to start.
I've done tasks like this well before.

results.name: Apathy Zone
results.text: Low challenge, low skill: easy to drift and scroll. Pick one tiny goal that stretches you just a bit, and start there.

C.name: Anxiety Zone
C.text: The task is bigger than your current skill. Shrink it: break it into one piece you can do, or get a quick lesson first.

S.name: Boredom Zone
S.text: You're better than the task. Raise the bar: add a time limit, a quality goal, or a harder version.

CS.name: Flow Channel
CS.text: High challenge meets high skill. This is where time disappears. Protect it: phone away, one clear goal.

cards.insight: Csikszentmihalyi found that people feel most absorbed when a high challenge meets matching skill and the goal is clear. Too easy feels dull; too hard feels stressful. Later studies back the link but find it weaker than the classic picture suggests.
cards.model: Flow = challenge slightly above skill + clear goal + quick feedback.
cards.try_today: Pick one task and tweak it: a bit harder if bored, smaller if stressed. Then do 10 minutes with your phone away.

source.work: Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience (1990)

cards.hook: Your last focus session flopped. Which flow ingredient was missing?
cards.title: The Four Flow Ingredients

questions.q: When I sit down to work, I know exactly what 'done' looks like.
I can tell within minutes if I'm on the right track.
My usual tasks feel neither too easy nor too hard.
I can work 25 minutes without checking my phone or messages.
People or alerts rarely break my focus.

advice.0: Lowest on clear goal? Before starting, write one line: 'Done means…'. Vague goals are a top flow-killer.
advice.1: Lowest on feedback? Build a check: a test, a word count, a friend's quick look. Flow needs to see progress.
advice.2: Lowest on difficulty fit? Adjust the task: add a constraint if it's dull, split it if it's overwhelming.
advice.3: Lowest on interruptions? Put your phone in another room for one 25-minute block. Switching tasks leaves your mind half elsewhere.

cards.insight: Flow isn't luck. Csikszentmihalyi's research points to a few conditions that make it likely: a clear goal, fast feedback, a challenge that fits your skill, and deep focus. Your weakest ingredient is usually the quickest fix.
cards.model: Don't chase flow. Set up its conditions and let it arrive.
cards.try_today: Fix your weakest ingredient, then work for 10 focused minutes and notice how it felt.

source.work: Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience (1990)

cards.hook: You're lost in London. Want the satellite photo or the tube map?
cards.title: The Map Is Not the Territory

game.prompt: You need to get across London fast. You can take one: a perfect satellite photo of every street, or the famous tube map that bends rivers and squashes distances. Which gets you there?
game.reveal: For most trips, the tube map wins. It's 'wrong' about distance and geography on purpose: it throws away detail so you can act. Every map you carry in your head works the same way.

cards.insight: A more accurate map isn't always a better one. Your beliefs about people, money and yourself are maps too: simplified, partly wrong, useful for some trips and useless for others. The skill is knowing which trip you're on.
cards.model: Every belief is a map. Ask 'useful for what?' before asking 'true or false?'
cards.try_today: Pick one firm belief about yourself. Write one situation where that map works and one where it would get you lost.

source.work: Science and Sanity (1933); Box, 'Science and Statistics' (1976)

cards.hook: Your bathroom scale tells the truth, right? Swipe and see.
cards.title: Map or Territory?

game.prompt: Is this the thing itself, or a description of it?

items.text: The number on your bathroom scale
items.why: A reading of your body, not your body. It ignores muscle, water, and how you feel.

items.text: The rain falling on you right now
items.why: That's the thing itself. You can't argue with it, only respond.

items.text: A friend's 5-star restaurant review
items.why: Their compressed experience. Your night there may differ.

items.text: Your 'I'm bad at maths' story
items.why: A summary of some past moments, not a fact about every future one.

items.text: The taste of the coffee in your mouth
items.why: Direct experience. The menu description was the map.

items.text: Your GPA or performance score
items.why: A useful number that leaves out most of what you actually did.

cards.insight: Most of what we react to is a map: numbers, labels, stories, reviews. They're handy, but they leave things out. When a map upsets you, check the territory before you act.
cards.model: When a label stings, ask: is this the thing, or a description of the thing?
cards.try_today: Next time a number or label bothers you today, name one important thing it leaves out.

source.work: Science and Sanity (1933)

cards.hook: A person in a gorilla suit walks past. Would you notice? Guess.
cards.title: You See What You Aim At

game.question: People watch a short video and count basketball passes. A person in a gorilla suit walks through the middle of the scene. Roughly what % of viewers never notice the gorilla?
game.explain: In Simons & Chabris's 1999 study, 46% of viewers missed it overall (more in harder versions). Counting passes was the goal, so the gorilla went unseen.

cards.insight: Attention follows aims. When you hunt for one thing, your brain filters out a lot of the rest, even big, strange things. That's not a flaw; it's how focus works. But it means your goals quietly shape what you see.
cards.model: Your aim is a filter. Change what you're looking for and the world rearranges.
cards.try_today: Before your next walk or meeting, set a new aim: 'notice three things that are going well.' Then count them.

source.work: Simons & Chabris, Gorillas in Our Midst (1999); Peterson, Maps of Meaning (1999)

cards.hook: Your boss texts: 'Can we talk tomorrow?' What does your gut say?
cards.title: Reframing

steps.scenario: 9pm. Your manager texts: 'Can we talk tomorrow at 10?' No context. Your heart rate goes up. What do you tell yourself?

options.text: 'I'm in trouble. I should prepare for the worst.'
options.feedback: Totally normal first reaction. But it's one story out of many, and it will cost you a night's sleep before you know anything.

options.text: 'I don't know what this is yet. Could be a project, feedback, or news. I'll find out at 10.'
options.feedback: That's reappraisal: same facts, wider frame. You haven't lied to yourself, you've just stopped writing the ending early.

options.text: 'Whatever, I don't care.'
options.feedback: Pushing the feeling down often keeps it buzzing underneath. Research suggests suppression tends to work worse than reframing.

steps.scenario: Next morning, still nervous. What's a useful move?

options.text: Reply: 'Sure! Anything I should bring?'
options.feedback: Turns a vague threat into a concrete task. Often you'll get the context you were missing.

options.text: Replay worst cases until 10am
options.feedback: Understandable, but rumination rarely adds information. One small action usually helps more.

cards.insight: Events don't hit you raw; they arrive inside a frame. Changing the frame (not the facts) can change how your body reacts and what you do next. Research by James Gross and others finds reappraisal usually works better than suppression.
cards.model: Same facts, new frame: 'What else could this mean?' is the cheapest stress tool you own.
cards.try_today: When something stings today, write two other honest explanations for it before you react.

source.work: Gross & John, Individual differences in two emotion regulation processes (2003); Epictetus, Enchiridion

cards.hook: Your heart's pounding before a big talk. Enemy or fuel?
cards.title: Stress Mindset

questions.q: Before an exam or big moment, my racing heart means…
When work piles up, I mostly try to…
Looking back, stressful times in my life…
Feeling stressed is a sign that…

zones.label: Stress-is-harmful lens
zones.text: You read stress mostly as danger. That's understandable, and sometimes right. Try adding one more reading: 'my body is getting me ready.'

zones.label: Mixed lens
zones.text: You see both sides. Next time, notice which story you pick in the moment. You often get to choose.

zones.label: Stress-can-fuel lens
zones.text: You tend to read stress as energy. Keep it, and still watch for real overload: rest is part of the deal.

cards.insight: In Alia Crum's studies, people taught to see stress as enhancing reported better performance and health than those shown its harms. The effect is real but modest, and chronic or severe stress still deserves real support, not just a new mindset.
cards.model: Stress has a meaning you assign. 'My body is gearing up' beats 'I'm breaking.'
cards.try_today: Before your next nervous moment, take one slow breath and tell yourself: 'This is energy for something I care about.'

source.work: Crum, Salovey & Achor, Rethinking stress (2013); McGonigal, The Upside of Stress (2015)

cards.hook: 'I'm just not a people person.' How would you prove that?
cards.title: Pragmatic Truth

game.prompt: You believe 'I'm not a people person.' A pragmatist asks: what would you DO differently if it were true, and what happens when you live by it? Which test tells you more?
choices: Thinking hard about whether it's really true
Living one week as if it might be false, then checking
game.reveal: William James and Charles Peirce argued an idea's meaning lies in its practical consequences. Live by it, see what happens. A belief that keeps you home alone 'proves itself' only because you never ran the test.

cards.insight: Pragmatism asks a practical question: what happens when you act on this idea? Some beliefs make your life bigger, some smaller. This is a philosophical lens, not a lab finding, and it doesn't mean facts don't matter. It means test beliefs in action.
cards.model: Judge a belief by its consequences: run the experiment, then decide.
cards.try_today: Pick one limiting belief. Do one small action that would only make sense if it were false. Note what actually happened.

source.work: James, Pragmatism (1907); Peirce, How to Make Our Ideas Clear (1878)

cards.hook: Your lens might be fogged in one spot. Find out which in 30 sec.
cards.title: Your Perception Loop

questions.q: I notice details others miss, including small signs things are changing.
I often realise later that I missed something obvious.
When something goes wrong, I can come up with more than one explanation.
My first read of a situation usually feels like the only one.
When I'm proven wrong, I update my view fairly quickly.
I keep doing what I've always done, even when results disappoint.

results.name: Running on Autopilot
results.text: Right now the loop is mostly quiet, which happens when we're tired or busy. Start with Perceive: spend one minute a day noticing three new things.

P.name: The Noticer
P.text: You see a lot, but you may lock into the first story and keep doing the same thing. Your fogged spots: Appraise and Recalibrate. Ask 'what else could this mean?'

A.name: The Interpreter
A.text: You're good at re-reading situations, but may be working from thin data and slow to change course. Gather one more fact before deciding.

R.name: The Adapter
R.text: You change course readily. Check that you're adjusting to real signals, not noise: slow down to notice and interpret first.

AP.name: The Analyst
AP.text: You see clearly and think flexibly, but insight may not turn into change. Your fogged spot is Recalibrate: make one small adjustment this week.

PR.name: The Reactor
PR.text: You spot change and move fast, but may jump on the first interpretation. Your fogged spot is Appraise: pause for a second explanation.

AR.name: The Theorist-in-Motion
AR.text: You reframe and adapt well, but may be missing inputs. Your fogged spot is Perceive: ask someone what they see that you don't.

APR.name: Calibrated Loop
APR.text: All three are humming. Keep it honest by measuring results: a good loop checks itself against reality, not just feelings.

cards.insight: QUMNI's PCF treats your mind like a controller: perceive the world, appraise what it means, recalibrate, act, repeat. Most people are stronger at one or two steps. Your weakest step is where your view can quietly bend. A self-check, not a diagnosis.
cards.model: Perceive, appraise, recalibrate. Your weakest step is where your view of reality bends.
cards.try_today: Take one frustrating situation from this week and run it through your weakest step, on paper, in five minutes.

source.work: QUMNI Perceptual Control Framework; Powers, Behavior: The Control of Perception (1973)

cards.hook: A thermostat is smarter than most New Year's resolutions. Why?
cards.title: Perceive, Adjust, Repeat

game.prompt: Put the PCF loop in order, the way a good controller (or a good mind) runs it.
items: Perceive what's actually happening
Appraise what it means for your goal
Recalibrate your model or plan
Act
Measure the result, then repeat
game.explain: A thermostat senses, compares to its target, adjusts, and checks again, forever. Many resolutions stall because they skip 'measure and adjust.' Perceptual Control Theory (Powers, 1973) describes living things as running loops like this.

cards.insight: Good controllers don't need a perfect plan. They need a fast loop: notice, compare, adjust, act, check. Your habits, relationships and goals improve the same way: small corrections, often.
cards.model: Don't aim for a perfect plan. Aim for a fast, honest feedback loop.
cards.try_today: Pick one goal. Set a 2-minute check-in tonight: what happened, what does it mean, what will I adjust tomorrow?

source.work: Powers, Behavior: The Control of Perception (1973); QUMNI Perceptual Control Framework

cards.hook: Is your week snowballing, or quietly snapping back to normal?
cards.title: Snowball or Thermostat?

game.prompt: Does this loop grow itself, or pull back to a set point?

items.text: Money in savings earns interest, which earns more interest
items.why: Growth feeds more growth. Classic reinforcing loop.

items.text: You feel hungry, eat, and the hunger goes away
items.why: Your body pulls you back toward a set point. That's balancing.

items.text: A rumor spreads: the more people know, the more people tell
items.why: Each new teller makes more tellers, whether the rumor is true or false.

items.text: You speed up when late, slow down once you're on time
items.why: The gap to a goal drives the action, and the action closes the gap.

items.text: Short on sleep, you scroll late to unwind, then sleep even less
items.why: Tired leads to scrolling leads to more tired. Vicious circles are reinforcing too.

items.text: Practicing makes it easier, so you practice more
items.why: Virtuous circle: skill makes practice pleasant, practice builds skill.

cards.insight: Almost everything that changes over time runs on two loops. Reinforcing loops amplify whatever is happening, good or bad. Balancing loops resist change and hold things near a target. Knowing which one you're in tells you whether to feed it or break it.
cards.model: Reinforcing loops snowball; balancing loops hold a set point. Ask which one is running.
cards.try_today: Write one habit you want as a loop: 'A makes B, B makes more A.' Find the arrow you can strengthen today.

source.work: Thinking in Systems: A Primer (2008)

cards.hook: One skipped walk can turn into a lost month. Can you trace how?
cards.title: Trace the Vicious Circle

game.prompt: Put this downward spiral in order, then spot where to cut it
items: You skip your walk because you feel low on energy
You move less, so you sleep a bit worse
Worse sleep leaves you with even less energy
Low energy makes skipping the next walk feel reasonable
The loop repeats, a little stronger each lap
game.explain: Each step makes the next one more likely, so the circle feeds itself. The same structure can run in reverse: a short, easy walk can be the step that starts the upward version.

cards.insight: Spirals can feel like bad luck or a flaw in you, but they're often just a loop. Once you draw the circle, you can see each link where a small change helps. You don't need to fix it all, just one arrow.
cards.model: If it keeps getting worse (or better) on its own, look for the circle, then cut or feed one link.
cards.try_today: Sketch one loop in your life as 4 boxes and arrows. Circle the easiest link and change just that one today.

source.work: The Fifth Discipline (1990)

cards.hook: Why do you always end up scalding, then freezing, in a new shower?
cards.title: The Shower Problem

steps.scenario: Hotel shower. Water is cold. You turn the knob toward hot. Five seconds later it's still cold. You…

options.text: Crank it much hotter. It clearly isn't working.
options.feedback: Very human, and exactly how you get scalded. The hot water was already in the pipe, on its way.

options.text: Wait a few more seconds before touching it again
options.feedback: Yes. The pipe adds a delay. Give your last action time to show its result.

options.text: Give up and take a cold shower
options.feedback: Brave, but the system was working. It was just slow to report back.

steps.scenario: Three weeks into a new workout plan, you don't feel much different yet. You…

options.text: Double the intensity to force results
options.feedback: That's the shower move again. Overcorrecting raises the risk of injury or burnout.

options.text: Keep the plan and judge it again after 8 weeks
options.feedback: Bodies, skills, and relationships all respond with a lag. Set a fair review date.

options.text: Switch to a totally different plan
options.feedback: Switching resets the clock before the first plan could show anything.

cards.insight: When results lag behind actions, it's easy to think nothing is happening and push harder. Then the delayed results land and we overshoot. Many problems in health, money, and teams are delay problems, not effort problems.
cards.model: Slow feedback plus impatience equals overshoot. Act, wait for the lag, then adjust.
cards.try_today: Pick one thing you're trying to improve. Write down how long it fairly takes to show results, and put a review date in your calendar.

source.work: The Fifth Discipline (1990); Sterman, Business Dynamics (2000)

cards.hook: Most people push where change is hardest. Can you find the lever?
cards.title: Where to Push

game.prompt: Rank these places to change a system, from weakest to strongest lever
items: Numbers (budgets, targets, quantities)
Feedback loops (how strongly the system self-corrects)
Information (who sees what, when)
Rules (incentives, permissions, punishments)
Goals (what the system is actually trying to do)
Mindset (the shared beliefs the whole system grows from)
game.explain: Donella Meadows ranked 12 places to intervene. Tweaking numbers is the easiest and usually the weakest. Changing goals and mindsets is harder, but it changes everything downstream.

cards.insight: Adjusting numbers (more hours, bigger targets) rarely changes how a system behaves. Changing who sees what, the rules, or the goal often moves far more with less force. Meadows called her list a work in progress, not a law.
cards.model: Numbers are easy and weak. Information, rules, and goals are harder and strong.
cards.try_today: Pick one stuck problem. Instead of 'more' or 'less' of something, write one change to its rules, information, or goal.

source.work: Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System (1999)

cards.hook: When stuck, do you try harder or change the game? Find out.
cards.title: Tweaker or Redesigner?

questions.q: You keep spending too much. Your first move is…

options.label: Promise to be stricter with myself
Lower my spending target a bit
Make savings move automatically on payday

questions.q: Your team keeps missing deadlines. You…

options.label: Make progress visible to everyone each week
Ask what the team is really rewarded for

questions.q: You want to read more. You…

options.label: Put a book where your phone usually sits
Just try to remember to read

questions.q: An argument with a partner keeps repeating. You…

options.label: Try to win it more clearly next time
Ask what each of you is actually trying to protect

zones.label: Tweaker
zones.text: You reach for effort and numbers first. That's honest work, but it can be exhausting. Next time, ask: what rule, information, or goal is producing this?

zones.label: Mixed
zones.text: You switch between pushing harder and redesigning. Notice which one you pick under stress, and try the redesign first once this week.

zones.label: Redesigner
zones.text: You look for the structure behind the problem. Keep going, and remember that redesigns also need patience while the results catch up.

cards.insight: Willpower and bigger targets are often weak levers, yet they're the first we grab. Changing what you see, what's rewarded, or what you aim at tends to work with less strain. Knowing your default lets you choose on purpose.
cards.model: Before pushing harder, ask what structure is producing the result.
cards.try_today: Take one 'I should try harder' and rewrite it as a change to your surroundings, rules, or reminders. Do that change now.

source.work: Thinking in Systems: A Primer (2008)

cards.hook: A city paid people per rat tail. Guess what it got more of.
cards.title: The Rat Tail Bounty

game.prompt: Hanoi, 1902. Rats are spreading through the new sewers, so officials pay a small bounty for every rat tail handed in. What happens next?
game.reveal: It backfired. People were seen with tailless rats still alive, so rats could keep breeding, and there were reports of rats being farmed for tails. Historian Michael Vann documented the episode. The fix rewarded tails, not fewer rats.

cards.insight: A quick fix relieves the symptom today, then its side effects quietly feed the original problem tomorrow. Because the side effect is delayed, the fix looks like it works, so we do it again. The pattern shows up in diets, deadlines, and arguments.
cards.model: Ask of every fix: what does this reward, and what will it feed in three months?
cards.try_today: Name one quick fix you use often (snacking, cramming, avoiding). Write what it might be feeding in the long run.

source.work: The Fifth Discipline (1990); Vann, 'Of Rats, Rice, and Race' (2003)

cards.hook: What's your crutch quietly doing to the muscle underneath?
cards.title: Crutch or Muscle?

game.prompt: Does this treat the symptom, or build the real capacity?

items.text: A third coffee every afternoon to get through the slump
items.why: It works today, but it can hurt tonight's sleep, which deepens tomorrow's slump.

items.text: Moving bedtime 20 minutes earlier
items.why: If short sleep is behind the slump, this goes after the cause, not the feeling.

items.text: Letting a coworker always handle your hard emails
items.why: Relief now, but your own skill and confidence never get the reps.

items.text: Drafting the hard email yourself and asking for feedback
items.why: Uncomfortable, but each try builds the skill you were avoiding.

items.text: Using autocorrect for a word you never learn to spell
items.why: Harmless here. Not every crutch is bad; just know which muscle you're skipping.

items.text: Asking a teacher to explain the step you keep getting wrong
items.why: Help that teaches is the opposite of a crutch: it shrinks your need for help.

cards.insight: When a quick fix keeps solving a problem for you, the ability to solve it yourself can weaken, so you need the fix even more. Help isn't the problem; help that replaces learning is. Often the best move is to use the crutch and train the muscle at the same time.
cards.model: Use help that teaches. Watch for fixes you need more each month.
cards.try_today: Pick one thing you always outsource or avoid. Do one small piece of it yourself today, with support nearby if you need it.

source.work: The Fifth Discipline (1990)

cards.hook: A bat and ball cost $1.10. Your gut already has an answer. Check it.
cards.title: Fast & Slow Thinking

game.question: Bat + ball = $1.10. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How many cents is the ball?
game.explain: If the ball were 10¢, the bat would be $1.10 and the total $1.20. Ball 5¢ + bat $1.05 = $1.10. Most people's first answer is 10¢, including many students at top universities.

cards.insight: The 10¢ answer arrives instantly and feels right. That's your fast mind: quick, effortless, usually helpful. The slow mind only steps in when you make it check. Being smart doesn't switch it on; pausing does.
cards.model: Fast thinking proposes, slow thinking checks. When it feels obvious and matters, check once.
cards.try_today: Say your gut answer out loud before your next decision that matters, then ask: 'How would I check this?'

source.work: Cognitive Reflection and Decision Making (2005); Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011)

cards.hook: Hare or owl: who's actually making your decisions this week?
cards.title: Who's Driving: Hare or Owl?

questions.q: A message annoys you. You usually…
Buying something over $100, you…
When a headline makes you angry, you…
Someone asks: 'Quick, what's 17 × 24?' You…

options.label: Work it out step by step

zones.label: Hare-led
zones.text: Your fast mind drives a lot. That's efficient for routine stuff. For the few decisions that matter, add one deliberate pause.

zones.label: Shared driving
zones.text: You switch between speeds. The skill now is noticing which moments deserve the owl.

zones.label: Owl-led
zones.text: You slow down a lot. Great for big calls. Watch for overthinking small, reversible ones; your hare is good at those.

cards.insight: Neither speed is 'better'. The fast mind handles most of life well; it slips on numbers, anger, and novelty. 'System 1 and 2' are a metaphor, not two brain parts. Kahneman said so himself.
cards.model: Let the hare handle the routine; call the owl for anything costly, emotional, or new.
cards.try_today: Pick one trigger (an angry message, a purchase over a set amount) and make it your rule to wait 10 minutes first.

source.work: Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011)

cards.hook: We'll show you a random number first. Watch it bend your guess.
cards.title: Anchoring

game.question: What percentage of UN member countries are in Africa?
game.explain: 54 of the 193 UN members are African: about 28%. In a famous 1974 study, people who first saw a wheel land on 65 guessed a median of 45%; those who saw 10 guessed 25%. The random number pulled their answers.

cards.insight: A number you know is irrelevant still drags your estimate toward it. Salespeople, salary talks, and 'was $199, now $99' tags all use this. Knowing about it helps a little; preparing your own number helps more.
cards.model: The first number sets the field. Bring your own number before you hear theirs.
cards.try_today: Write your own number down before your next price, salary, or deadline talk, with one reason it's fair.

source.work: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (1974)

cards.hook: Your brain ranks dangers by how easily they come to mind. Test it.
cards.title: Availability Bias

game.prompt: Compared to how often it feels like it happens…

items.text: Dying in a plane crash
items.why: Crashes get huge coverage. Per mile, commercial flying is far safer than driving.

items.text: Being killed by a shark
items.why: Worldwide, unprovoked shark deaths are usually in single digits per year.

items.text: Older adults dying after a fall
items.why: Falls are a leading cause of injury death for people over 65. Quiet, rarely in the news.

items.text: A child taken by a total stranger
items.why: Stranger abductions are very rare; most missing children are runaways or family cases.

items.text: Heart disease as a cause of death
items.why: It's the top cause of death worldwide (WHO), yet rarely makes headlines.

items.text: Car crashes
items.why: About 1.2 million road deaths a year worldwide (WHO). So routine they're barely news.

cards.insight: Vivid, recent, or dramatic events are easy to recall, so they feel frequent. Slow, ordinary risks hide. Your news feed is a highlight reel of rare events, not a map of real risk.
cards.model: Easy to imagine is not the same as likely. Ask for the count, not the story.
cards.try_today: Look up one number the next time a scary story grabs you: how many times a year does this actually happen?

source.work: Availability: A Heuristic for Judging Frequency and Probability (1973)

cards.hook: 2, 4, 6 follows a secret rule. Most people's first guess is wrong.
cards.title: Confirmation Bias

steps.scenario: The numbers 2-4-6 follow a hidden rule. You can test any three numbers and learn if they fit. Your hunch: 'even numbers going up by 2.' Which test teaches you the most?

options.feedback: It fits, but it would fit your hunch either way. You'd learn nothing new. This is what most people try.
Another yes, but again only a test your hunch already predicts. Confirming feels productive; it rarely is.
Yes! Your hunch says 'no'. If it fits, your hunch is wrong. That's a real test. Spoiler: it fits.

options.text: Just guess the rule now
options.feedback: Bold! But without a test that could prove you wrong, you'd be guessing blind.

steps.scenario: 1-2-3 fits. So does 3-17-90. 6-4-2 does not. What's the rule?

options.text: Any three numbers going up
options.feedback: Correct. In Wason's 1960 study, only about 1 in 5 people named it on their first try, mostly because they only tested examples they expected to fit.

options.text: Numbers with a pattern
options.feedback: Close in spirit, but 3-17-90 has no neat pattern. Simpler: they just go up.

options.text: Even numbers only
options.feedback: 1-2-3 fit, so odd numbers are allowed. The rule is broader: any rising sequence.

cards.insight: We tend to test ideas in ways that can only say 'yes'. That feels like evidence but often isn't. Researchers still debate how irrational this is, but the fix is clear: look for the result that would prove you wrong.
cards.model: Don't ask 'what fits my idea?' Ask 'what would I see if I were wrong?'
cards.try_today: Pick one belief you hold firmly. Write down one thing that, if you saw it, would change your mind. Go look for it.

source.work: On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task (1960)

cards.hook: In an argument, are you defending a fort or drawing a map?
cards.title: Soldier or Scout?

questions.q: Someone shares a study that disagrees with you. First thought:
When did you last change your mind on something you cared about?
Your feed mostly shows people who…

options.label: I follow some smart critics on purpose

questions.q: Being proven wrong feels like…

zones.label: Soldier mode
zones.text: You guard your views well, which is very human. Try treating one belief as a draft, not a fort.

zones.label: Switching
zones.text: You scout on some topics and defend on others. Notice which ones make you defensive; that's where your map is least checked.

zones.label: Scout mode
zones.text: You're curious about being wrong. Keep it kind: scouts share maps, they don't sneer at others' wrong turns.

cards.insight: Everyone slips into defending. The scout mindset isn't about being less passionate. It's about wanting your map to be accurate more than you want to be right. Your answers here are a snapshot, not a verdict.
cards.model: A soldier asks 'Can I believe this?' or 'Must I believe this?' A scout asks 'Is it true?'
cards.try_today: In your next disagreement, ask one honest question: 'What would change your mind?' Then answer it yourself too.

source.work: The Scout Mindset (2021)

cards.hook: Heads you win $150, tails you lose $100. Do you flip?
cards.title: Loss Aversion

game.prompt: One fair coin flip. Heads: you win $150. Tails: you lose $100. On average this bet pays you $25. Do you take it?
game.reveal: Most people say no. In Kahneman's studies, people typically want a win of about $200 before risking $100. Losses tend to feel roughly 1.5–2.5× as strong as equal gains.

cards.insight: Turning down a good bet isn't wrong when the loss would truly hurt you. But we often avoid small, smart risks just because losing stings. Some researchers argue the effect is smaller than claimed, especially for small amounts.
cards.model: Losses shout, gains whisper. For small, repeatable bets, judge the average, not the sting.
cards.try_today: Name one small risk you've avoided (asking, applying, trying). Write the realistic worst case. Is it really that bad?

source.work: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk (1979)

cards.hook: Stuck on how to succeed? Plan how to fail instead.
cards.title: Inversion

game.prompt: Put the inversion moves in order
items: Name what you want (e.g. a good friendship)
Ask: how could I guarantee it fails?
List the answers (cancel often, only talk about me…)
Circle the ones you already do a little
Stop one of them this week
game.explain: Thinking backward makes hidden mistakes obvious. It's often easier to list ways to ruin something than ways to perfect it, and avoiding stupidity is a solid path to doing well.

cards.insight: Mathematician Carl Jacobi is credited with 'invert, always invert'. Investor Charlie Munger made it a life habit. Your brain finds failure modes faster than success recipes; use that.
cards.model: Ask what would guarantee failure, then don't do that.
cards.try_today: Pick one goal. Write 3 ways to guarantee it fails. Circle the one you're closest to doing, and drop it today.

source.work: Poor Charlie's Almanack (2005)

cards.hook: A city paid people per rat tail. Guess what they got more of.
cards.title: Second-Order Thinking

steps.scenario: Hanoi, 1902. Rats are spreading. Officials pay a small reward for every rat tail handed in. What happens next?

options.text: The rat problem shrinks
options.feedback: That's the first-order guess, and it's what officials expected. Reality had a twist.

options.text: People cut off tails and let rats go to breed
options.feedback: Yes. Tailless rats were seen in the streets, and some people reportedly bred rats for the bounty.

options.text: Nobody bothers to collect tails
options.feedback: The opposite. People collected lots of tails, just not in the way that helped.

steps.scenario: You want your team to fix bugs faster, so you plan to reward 'bugs fixed per week'. Ask 'and then what?' twice. Best tweak?

options.text: Reward bugs fixed, bigger bonus
options.feedback: More pressure on the same number. People may ship sloppy code and fix their own bugs later.

options.text: Track fewer bugs reaching users, and talk about it
options.feedback: Good. You reward the real goal and keep a human check, so gaming it is harder.

options.text: Don't measure anything
options.feedback: Understandable after the rats! But you can measure well; just ask what the number will make people do.

cards.insight: First-order thinking asks 'what happens now?' Second-order asks 'and then what?' Rewards change behavior, often in ways no one planned. Historian Michael Vann documented the Hanoi rat hunt.
cards.model: Every fix creates new incentives. Ask 'and then what?' at least twice.
cards.try_today: Write 'and then what?' before your next rule, rule-change, or reward, and answer it two times.

source.work: The Most Important Thing (2011); Of Rats, Rice, and Race (2003)

cards.hook: A test says you have a rare condition. How worried should you be?
cards.title: Base Rates

game.question: A condition affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test catches every real case but gives a false positive to 5% of healthy people. You test positive. Chance you have it?
game.explain: Of 1,000 people: 1 truly has it. About 50 healthy people also test positive. So 1 of ~51 positives is real: about 2%. In a 1978 study, many doctors and students at Harvard hospitals guessed 95%.

cards.insight: The test result is vivid; the rarity is quiet. When something is rare, most positives are false alarms, which is why doctors confirm with a second test. Real results need a real doctor; this is just the math.
cards.model: Start with how common it is, then adjust for the new evidence. Rare things stay fairly rare.
cards.try_today: Ask 'Out of 1,000 similar cases, how many usually turn out this way?' the next time a story or alarm surprises you.

source.work: Interpretation by Physicians of Clinical Laboratory Results (1978)

cards.hook: Half of what you worried about today was never yours to fix.
cards.title: Up to Me, or Not?

game.prompt: Is it up to you?

items.text: Whether your train is late
items.why: Timetables, weather, signals. Real, but not in your hands.

items.text: Leaving 10 minutes earlier next time
items.why: Your choice, fully. This is where the energy should go.

items.text: What your boss thinks of your idea
items.why: You can shape it, but their mind is theirs. Aim at the pitch, not the verdict.

items.text: How clearly you explain your idea
items.why: Preparation and clarity are yours. That's the part worth practising.

items.text: Whether you win the match
items.why: Opponents, luck and refs get a vote. The Stoics called outcomes 'not up to us'.

items.text: How hard you train this week
items.why: Effort and attitude belong to you. Epictetus put judgments and actions here.

items.text: Your first emotional jolt when insulted
items.why: The flash is fast and automatic. What you do in the next minute is yours.

cards.insight: You just split life into two piles. Epictetus argued that most suffering comes from pouring effort into the left pile. Notice the trick: almost every 'not up to me' outcome has an 'up to me' action hiding next to it.
cards.model: Care about outcomes, but aim your effort at your own choices, judgments and actions.
cards.try_today: Write your biggest worry. Under it, list two actions that are fully up to you. Do one before tonight.

source.work: Enchiridion (c. 125 CE)

cards.hook: Your flight is cancelled. 200 angry people. What's your first move?
cards.title: The Stoic at the Gate

steps.scenario: The board flips to CANCELLED. A crowd forms at the desk. You…

options.text: Join the queue and tell everyone how unacceptable this is.
options.feedback: Totally human. But the anger costs you energy and changes nothing about the plane.

options.text: Open the airline app and rebook while you stand in line.
options.feedback: You spotted the part that's yours: options, timing, your next move. The queue stays a backup.

options.text: Sit down and wait for someone to announce a plan.
options.feedback: Calm is good. Pair it with one small action and you'll often get a better seat sooner.

steps.scenario: The agent says the next flight is tomorrow. You feel heat in your chest. You…

options.text: Breathe, then ask: 'What are my options for tonight?'
options.feedback: Same disappointment, better question. Calm, specific asks usually get more help than blame.

options.text: Tell the agent this is their fault.
options.feedback: Understandable, but they didn't cancel the plane. Blame aimed at the wrong target rarely pays.

options.text: Say nothing and walk off fuming.
options.feedback: You protected the agent, which is kind. Try naming one thing you can still do tonight.

cards.insight: You didn't stop caring about getting home. You moved your effort from the cancelled plane to the phone in your hand and the question you asked. That shift is the Stoic dichotomy of control, in real time.
cards.model: When something goes wrong, ask: what's the next move that is fully mine?
cards.try_today: Next time something annoys you, say out loud "What's mine here?" and do that one thing first.

source.work: Enchiridion (c. 125 CE)

cards.hook: Do you spend your week on what you can change, or what you can't?
cards.title: Your Circle of Influence

questions.q: When the economy news is bad, I mostly…

options.label: Read more about it and feel worse
Check my own budget and skills

questions.q: When a teammate keeps missing deadlines, I…

options.label: Ask them what's getting in the way

questions.q: My most common sentence starts with…
When I'm stuck, I first look for…

options.label: Who or what is to blame
The smallest thing I could change

zones.label: Concern-heavy
zones.text: A lot of your energy goes to things you can't move. That's tiring, not a flaw. Pick one worry and find the piece of it that is yours.

zones.label: Split
zones.text: You switch between worrying and acting. Notice which topics pull you outward and give those a small action.

zones.label: Influence-focused
zones.text: You aim at what you can move. Covey's claim is that this circle grows as you use it: trust and skill pile up.

cards.insight: Stephen Covey drew two circles: everything you care about, and the smaller part you can affect. Energy spent inside the smaller circle tends to grow it, because acting builds skill and trust. It's the Stoic idea with a practical twist.
cards.model: Work inside what you can influence, and that circle slowly gets bigger.
cards.try_today: Swap one "If only they…" sentence today for "I can…" and finish it with a real action.

source.work: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989)

cards.hook: Too timid or too reckless? Four answers will place your courage.
cards.title: The Golden Mean

questions.q: Someone in a meeting says something you think is wrong. You…

options.label: Stay quiet, it's not worth it
Ask a calm question about it
Call it out bluntly on the spot

questions.q: A friend invites you on a hard hike you've never done. You…

options.label: Say yes and check the route and weather
Go in trainers, no water, figure it out

questions.q: You have a business idea. You…

options.label: Keep it in a notebook for 'someday'
Quit your job tomorrow to do it

questions.q: Someone is being mocked in a group chat. You…

options.label: Message them privately, then say 'not cool' in the chat
Post a long public rant at the mocker

zones.label: Leaning cautious
zones.text: Caution protects you, and sometimes it costs you. Try one small, safe step past your comfort line this week.

zones.label: Near the mean
zones.text: You aim for the middle path Aristotle called courage: brave enough to act, wise enough to prepare.

zones.label: Leaning bold
zones.text: Your energy is a gift. Adding one check before you leap turns boldness into courage.

cards.insight: Aristotle said a virtue sits between two vices: too little and too much. Courage lives between cowardice and recklessness. The middle isn't the average or lukewarm; it's the right amount for this situation.
cards.model: Virtue is calibration: the right action, in the right amount, at the right time.
cards.try_today: Pick one choice today and ask: what would 'too little' and 'too much' look like here? Then do the in-between.

source.work: Nicomachean Ethics (c. 340 BCE)

cards.hook: Are you an above-average driver? Guess how many people say yes.
cards.title: Knowing You Don't Know

game.question: In a classic study, what % of US drivers rated themselves more skilful than the median driver?
game.explain: Svenson (1981) found about 93% of a small US student sample rated themselves more skilful than the median driver. At most 50% can be.

cards.insight: Most of us rate ourselves above average, which can't all be true. Socrates thought wisdom began with admitting what you don't know. The famous Dunning-Kruger curve is debated, but over-confidence itself is well documented.
cards.model: Treat your confidence as a guess, not a fact. 'I might be wrong' opens the door to learning.
cards.try_today: Pick one opinion you hold strongly. Write the best reason someone could disagree with it, in their words, not yours.

source.work: Plato, Apology (c. 399 BCE); Svenson, Acta Psychologica (1981)

cards.hook: A setback you got through: would you delete it from your story?
cards.title: Amor Fati: Love Your Fate

game.prompt: Pick a real setback from your past: a rejection, a failure, a loss you've recovered from. If a button could erase it, and everything it led to, would you press it?
game.reveal: There's no wrong answer, and some pain is never 'worth it'. But many people find a setback also taught them a skill, a friend, or a direction. Nietzsche called embracing your whole story, hard parts included, amor fati.

cards.insight: Amor fati isn't pretending bad things were good. Nietzsche went far: he wanted nothing to be different. You can start smaller, by asking what a hard chapter gave you. Marcus Aurelius pictured a fire that turns whatever falls in into flame.
cards.model: You can't change what happened. You can choose what it becomes part of.
cards.try_today: Write one setback and finish this line: "Because of it, I can now…". Keep it to one sentence.

source.work: The Gay Science (1882); Meditations (c. 170 CE)

cards.hook: What were you worried about on this date three years ago?
cards.title: This Too Shall Pass

game.prompt: Try it now: what was keeping you up at night roughly three years ago? Can you name it clearly?
game.reveal: Many people can't. Research on 'affective forecasting' shows we tend to overestimate how long bad events will hurt. Feelings are weather: real, sometimes heavy, but they move. If a heavy mood isn't lifting for weeks, talk to someone you trust.

cards.insight: Gilbert and Wilson found people often predict setbacks will sting longer and harder than they do. The Buddha and Heraclitus both taught that everything changes. That doesn't shrink today's pain; it reminds you it isn't permanent.
cards.model: Feelings and fortunes are weather, not climate. Ask how much this will matter in a year.
cards.try_today: When something stings today, write it down with the date. Set a reminder to reread it in 3 months.

source.work: Wilson & Gilbert, 'Affective Forecasting' (2005)

cards.hook: Would your weekly calendar match the speech at your 80th birthday?
cards.title: Begin With the End in Mind

questions.q: This week I gave real, undistracted time to people I love.
The people closest to me would say I show up for them.
This week I moved, slept and ate like someone I'd want to be at 80.
I spent time on work I'm proud of, not just busy with.
I did something this week that helped someone beyond my circle.
I learned or practised something that's stretching me.

advice.0: Relationships lowest? Book 20 phone-free minutes with one person this week.
advice.1: Health lowest? Pick one: a 15-minute walk, or lights out 30 minutes earlier tonight.
advice.2: Craft lowest? Block one focused hour on the work you'd want to be remembered for.
advice.3: Contribution lowest? Do one small useful thing for someone who can't repay you.
advice.4: Growth lowest? Choose one skill and practise it for 10 minutes today.

cards.insight: Covey suggested imagining your own funeral: what would you want people to say? Seneca made a similar point: we act as if time is endless. Your shape shows where today's choices match that picture and where they drift.
cards.model: Decide what you want said about you at the end, then plan this week backwards from it.
cards.try_today: Write three words you'd want people to use about you at 80. Put one action for each in this week's calendar.

source.work: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989); On the Shortness of Life (c. 49 CE)

cards.hook: How many weeks are in an 80-year life? Guess before you scroll.
cards.title: Your Life in Weeks

game.question: How many weeks are there in an 80-year life?
game.explain: 80 years × about 52.18 weeks ≈ 4,174. Oliver Burkeman built a whole book around this small number.

cards.insight: Many people guess far higher. About four thousand weeks feels short, and that's the point: it isn't meant to scare you, it's meant to sharpen you. Seneca argued life is long enough if you use it well.
cards.model: Time is finite and countable. Spend weeks the way you'd spend something precious.
cards.try_today: Pick this week's one most important thing, the one you'd regret skipping, and schedule it before anything else.

source.work: Four Thousand Weeks (2021); On the Shortness of Life (c. 49 CE)
